div.head: 2 ALMS McDOUGALL'S Pent SELF-RAISING FLOUR THIPBESST.
div.p: 2 ALMS McDOUGALL'S Pent SELF-RAISING FLOUR THIPBESST.
WAR CORRESPONDENT'S ESCAPE.
Witness of 29 Historic Battles.

No man living has had a more varied or more exciting career as a journalist than Mr. F. Scndamore. For many years be was special correspondent for •"rhe Times" and "Daily News," and he also figured in the wars of Turkey, the Soudan campaign, and, more recently, in the Boer War. Mr. Scudamore, during a record of twenty-nine historic battles, has, naturally, had many narrow and thrilling escapes. His most vital experience he described the other day at his home, M, Richmond Terrace, London, S.W. "Some time ago after escaping the dangers to which one is exposed in the hazardous trade of war,"said Mr.Scudamore, "I fell a victim to an evil--the evil of blood-poisoning —which Zam-buk,the well-known antiseptic balm, alone was able to expel. The blood-poisoning started I believe owing to the poisonous dye in some underclothing penetrating a small scratch or sore. I was treated by doctors in the usual way, and told to hope for the best ; but the inflammation, pain, and swelling did not appear to he relieved by their treatment. Ulcers broke out in ray feet and limbs, and for svmetime it was quite impos- sible for me to put my feet to the ground or get about. " My left leg, below the knee, had seventeen deep holes, into any one of which I could have put my thumb, while I bad no fewer than four- teen similar ulcers on the right leg. "Worn out with pain and lack of sleep, I yielded, in despair, at last, to the advice of a friend, to try Zam-buk, of which my friend gave the highest accounts. I applied this capital balm to the sores ad ulcers, and you may be surprised to hear that within one week the pain and inflammation had all gone, and the skin which had before so obstinately refused to heal, was now growing beautifully. After under a fortnight's plentiful use of the balm I had begun to be a sound wan again, as Zam-buk had completely banished complications from the blood-poisoning." In perfectly healing the thirty odd ulcers in Mr. Scudamore's limbs and making the tissue once more healthy and sound, Zam-buk accomplished what no mere ointment or embrocatien could do. Zam-buk is a rare concentration of Nature's heal- ing forces. Every borne needs a box.

EY FITZGERALD MOLLOY,
Author of "Just at Moonrise, " "Sweet is Revenge," "The Die of Destiny," "On 'Wheels of Fire," "How Came He Dead ? " &c.

The garden-party was attended by n crowd of actors. authors, and artists, with their wonderfully. dressed womenfolk, together with a sprinkling of smart people, amongst whom were a foreign Marchioness with a glaring complexion and copper coloured hair, a bankrupt baronet, and an Engliah Countess with a damaged reputation*: It had lasted through the long Sunday afternoon of a June day, but had lost nothing of that glaring I gaiety which wearied Madge Aubrey, who at the first opportunity, quietly and as she believed unobservedly left the terraces, where ices and strawberries were being eaten, and champagne and claret-cup were being drunk in illimitable quantities. ; At the far end of the lawn she found a wicker- work chair under the cool shade of a giant cedar. It was delightful, she thought, to sit here, solitary and in peace, apart from all that. noisy laughter and I inane chatter; for within a few yards of her the I Thames swept slowly and lazily past grassy banks, its sorfaCe sparkling, the blue of a cloudless sky reflected in its depths. She closed her eyes, that she might the MOM completely surrender herself to the drowsy and delicious peace that was so foreign to her life; but she had scarcely entered into the enchanted land of her day-dreams before she suddenly felt that some- one was near her—someone whose movements she had not heard, but of whose identity she had no doubt. She opened her eyes, and as she expected saw George Meadows standing beside her, his figure tall and straight, his grave, handsome face flushing slightly under his sunburnt skin, an expression of almost boyish timidity in his eyes. He bowed and hoped he had not disturbed her. "I saw you leave the terraces, and I ventured to follow you," he said frankly, glancing towards the seats scattered around. "I came away because it's so much quieter here. Won't you sit down ? " she said, pointing to a chair near her own. He obeyed her in silence. That he had some- thing to say was evident from his ardent glances, but that he found it difficult to express was no less plain. "Isn't it delightfully restful here?" she said, adding: "How I wish all my life could be like this.'

Here is excellent news of a Warrington roan baying bound out by personal experience that kidney disease can be cured. The great thing in kidney trouble is to take the right medicine at the right time. The right time is on the first appearance of any symptom of kidney trouble, such as Backache, Urinary Troubles, Watery Swellings round the ankles or beneath the oyes, or Gravel. The right thing to take is Doan's Pills, as this Warrington man did. Mr. H. Thomas, 97, Fox-street, Warrington, says "I have suffered with kidney complaint more or less all my life. It is in the family. Every now end then I would have to knock off work and stay at borne nntil the violence of the pains in the small of my back had worn off sufficiently for me to start wprk again. " The urinary system was out of order, the kidney secretions being thick and at times containing gravel. There were also headaches and giddiness, sometimes severely. "I tried Doan's pills and they proved highly bene- ficial in my case : they cleared the kidney secretions and eased the pains in my back. I've been first rate since using the medicine. Atter a pause that seemed interminable he said 4 "It waa not your fault; you could not know whatl T felt. It was I who sought you. But how I lringered for you; how I fed my hopes; how I let them master me." Ile had no idea that she suffered with a bitter- ness which the practice of her profession made her better able to control. For now that he had spoken, she realised for the first time that she loved him as she had never loved before; that willingly, joyously, she would have given up her art, fame, ambition, the world itself, to follow him, if she were free.
• Suddenly mastering himeelf,he rose, and holding out his hand said: "Gcod-bye. I don't think I could bear to see you again, now that I know—"

She was startled by his abruptness and overcome by the thought of never meeting him more. It was s pain she could not readily endure. "Won't you—don't you care to hear how it happened?" she said, with a touch of reproach.

"Care to hear? " he answered. "Why, the smallest thing that concerns you—l can't speak, or I shall say too much—ask too much." "I trust you, my friend ; I trust you," she said hurriedly, with something of fear—fear of herself— in her voice.

"You may; you may," he replied, understanding her. He sat down again and stolidly waited for her to begin. "When I was married I didn't know anything of life," she said. "You didn't love him? " "Oh, never!" she answered, as if surprised by the question. For a moment his eyes lost their look of misery. "I had lived all my life in the country with my mother in a very simple way, for her annuity was small ; and if we were sometimes pinched—well, it didn't matter, until she fell ill, when for the first time I began to understand the -value of money, seeing all it would buy for her. I was then barely eighteen, and had just met a man who was staying at the Rectory. He was a great traveller and very weal thy. " "Young?" "He was over forty, which seemed old age to me, so that when he paid me compliments I merely laughed at him." .

on ; go on," George Meadows said impa- tiently, as she paused. "One day he paid an unusually long visit to my mother, and when he had gone she told me he had proposed for me, that he was very rich, and that he had promised never to take me from her so long as she lived. She and he, and indeed everyone but myself from whom it was kept secret, knew ru.t. ph. could not live long_ When I burst put

crying she soothed me, anu loin me it woula ue an immense relief to know that if anything hap- ptned to her I should have a protector, and not be cast upon the world a pauper. I married him, and though that marriage has ruined my life, I cannot say I regret it, for all my mother's wants were liberally supplied' and she whose life had been very hard, as Ii learnt from the letters she left, had the happiness in her last days of knowing that I was provided for, She died within three months of my marriage. Then we left my native village." "And your husband?" "For a while he managed to conceal his real nature. He was a drunkard; he was vile in every way," she answered, her voice becoming suddenly hard. "I shrank from him, I loathed him, and within a year of my marriage I ran away from him to the only friend I had in the world—the true, good woman who, unknown to him, had loved my father and had remained single for his sake; the woman who has always acted as my chaperon." "Miss Crayshaw ?" _ . _ _ _

"Yes; she sheltered me, and my husband, who knew where I bad gone, did not care to claim me. He made her a small allowance for my board, for she was far from rich. I had left the jewels and my wedding ring behind me, and I felt humiliated at 'being obliged to accept his money. My most anxious desire was to earn enough to support myself, so that I need take nothing from hini." "But why did you select the stage?" "Because Miss Crayshaw thought I could act. You know, she is an artist, and that she designs theatrical costumes. She insisted on my taking lessons in elocution, and then she introduced me to a manager, who got me a small part in a play just starting on a provincial tour. After three years of hard work in the country I got a London engage- ment; and before twelve months ended a piece of good luck fell in my way, when a famous dramatist cast me for the leading part in his new comedy. From the drat night my name was made, and I suddenly discore,red that everyone had known And

sue erten out (tenant:l7. "I think," said prudent Miss Crayshaw, "we might slip out through that little green gate in the garden wall, and avoid the crowd. You can write to our hostess to-morrow, and explain that you had a headache. Once we are outside the grounds, we can easily find ydur carriage; so pull down your veil, dear, an-. 1 let us go." When the actress reached her home she hurried to her room, the door of which she locked, and then flinging herself, dressed as she was, on her bed, gave way to her grief, that seemed all the more violent for being so long restrained. Poor Miss Crayshaw, walking backwards and forwards in the softly-carpeted passage outside, listened compassionately to the choking sobs which lasted over an hour. She allowed another hour to pass before she asked the grief-stricken woman to open the door, and to drink the tea which the good-natured soul had specially brewed. Even then she made no attempt at consolation, though her heart was wrenched for her friend's sufferings, and its tender memories that had lain dormant for many a year were stirred o vitality. Next day Madge Aubrey had recovered her com- posure, and with that strong sense of duty which characterised her, sought to take up the ordinary course of her life. She: sat at the breakfast. table, though she could not eat, and immediately after-, words began to study a new part she was soon to play; her swimming eyes and twitching lips alone hinting at the battle that was being bravely fought. The day seemed intolerably long to herivet she would not see vieitors, nor go out; and wheirevening came the idea of acting became hateful to her for ti,ie first. time. He detested the theatre, the thought of her playing was repugnant to him, and she now shared his views. itsat she had to tram( or the interests of her manager and of her own future; so setting aside her feelings, she drove to the tinatre and went through her part with a power and a feeling that stirred her audience to enthusiastic delight. Thar the first two days the postman never, rang at her door that she did not start and grow impatient to see what he brought; but as no letter catno from George Meadows the rest were flung aside. She had expected—hoped—he would have sent her n word of farewell, their parting had been so abrupt, so brief; but no doubt he was right in keeping silence, only at that time a line from him would have fallen as balm on her heart, which was sorely bruised in the struggle. On the third morning, as she entered- the break- fast-room, she saw her friend at. the window, a puzzled expression on her face as she examined an • envelope. "It's a letter fer von directed under cover to
me; as ustml," ausk C.irdysifaw thikarked. "From--"
"From Mexico."

The actress started. "Ile has not written to me since I refused his money. What can he have to say ? God grant he is not coming back," she said, terrified by such a supposition. "The direction is not in his writing," her friend said, handing her the letter. Miss Aubrey took it, impatiently tore open the envelope, read the first few lines of the enclosure, and fell forward with a cry. Careful Miss Crayshaw put the letter away, rang the bell, and with the assistance of a maid, lifted her insensible charge on the sofa. When restoratives had partially done their work the chaperon read the letter, then in the hope of calming her ercite- ment, she drank a cup of tea. A moment later, and she wrote out a message directed to George Meadows, which she despatched in all haste to the nearest telegraph office. By the time this was done Miss Aubrey had begun to sob, in a low key at first, but subsequently with increasing, violence ; whilst her friend, not striving to restrain her, walked up and down the room, absorbed in her own thoughts, pausing every now and then to look out of the windows. When the actress had regained something of her usual calm the chaperon said to her : "I have sent for George Meadows." "Oh, how could you, how could you?" the actress asked, her face flushing. "But he won't get your message ; he is at sea by this time, for he told me he would be on his way to Australia before the week was over; and I shall never see him again --never, never," and fresh tears came into her eyes. At that instant Miss Crayshaw, hearing sounds of wheels, looked out to see a four-wheeled cab laden with luggage stop at the door. Another instant and George Meadows got out, looked up at the house, and with a bound, mounted the steps, three at a time, with the air of a schoolboy. "‘lle is here, my dear," she said triumphantly. . .

, . "0, auntie, don't let him come in," Madge Aubrey called out, as she sprang from the sofa and began to arrange her hair before a looking-glass. "Hemustn't see me like this." But unheeding her, the chaperon had hurried into the hall, where she met George Meadows, a look of amazement, inquiry, and hope on his face. In her confusion she could only say: "You got my telegram? "Yes, it was handed to me just as I was stepping into my cab on my way to Euston Station. My chip leaves Liverpool to-night," he answered. "I fear you may have to forfeit your ticket." "What do you mean? What has happened ? " he gasped, not understanding her; his mind too confused, to think.

"Her husband is dead." he repeated, as if doubtful that he had heard aright. "We only knew of it an hour ago ; his solicitors wrote to her." "Where is she? " lie asked. Miss CraYsliaw softly opened the door of the breakfast-room, and when lie had stumbled acrosa its threshold, closed it behind him, she remaining outside.
With one swift glance he searched the face of the woman he worshipped, when something in her eyes responding, he rushed forward and flung his arms round her.
Neither could speak for some seconds. "After all, you are ;nine," he said, "you are "I am yours," she answered, her face pressed against his heart. Lie bent down and kissed her rapturously.

EMEMMIMUMN

burden of the people about with them. They asked; What was the meaning of it all? Why was it part and parcel of the discipline of life ? What aas the obvious purpose for which it came ? And what would be the final results ? They did not ignore the larger problems. They knew there was the colour problem coming—a- problem the whole civilized world would have to face. There were problems affecting the interests of peace, sobriety and humanity throughout the world. They were limited by no narrow parochial spirit, but despite all, despite the fact that they had hundreds and thou- sands of bitter foes, they could still afford to be optimistic. Why ? Because they knew that truth was great and bound ultimately to prevail. The second element was its wonderful humanism. He did not moan humanitarianism. He did not mean humaneness, though they were growing humanitarian and increas- ingly humane. It was the spirit and love that gave birth to both—that which inspire i their humanitarianism and that which made for humaneness. In other words, their religion stood for kinship, and kinship with the whole of humanity. They were all brothers, and they stood for the raising of the savages and the coloured people to the same pinnacle they themselves had already attained. That delightful humanism made them feel how little, how paltry, their ecclesiastical differ- ences were as compared with the larger problem of humanity that bound them together. They must take heart and he hopeful. The sun had sot yet been put out. The flowers had not ceased to blow. The zephyrs had not ceased to fan their face. God was in heaven, and what was infinitely better, He was in the world with them, and therefore all was right. (Applause.) The Rev. C. FlAnvnY-Coolc said he took the idealist standpoint rather than the optimistic or pessimistic. Unless there was a great ideal before them, no matter how optimistic they might be, they were apt to go a little bit astray. but if their anchorage be the anchorage of great and lofty ideals, then no matter where they saw the tragedy or the joy, the dark or the sunshine, the pain or pleasure, having great ideals, they would be the anlhor of the mind in the stress and discipline of life. Mr. Matthews' cheery and optimistic words had found a living echo in their own heart. He (Mr. Cook) quite agreed that it was no use trying to hide up the ecclesiastical divisions that separated them. He was sick and tired of people talking about undenominationalism. They wanted stronger denominationalism, and they wanted also to be scrupulously careful they did not misinterpret each other's position or what each other said. In reviewing the past year one of the most painful things to him had been the removal of Mr. Monks. sen., to Southport. He (Mr. Cook) was sorry they had not had a public occasion on which to express as a church their regard and affection for Mr. Monks, and the deep grief they felt at his leaving them. They were glad he had gone where, in all probability, the evening of life would be lengthened out. They were glad he was looking so well, and they prayed for him a happy time during the closing years of a very busy life. On Sunday the Sunday school prizes were distributed by Miss Dorothy Monks, who took not only interest in the Girls' Club, but also in the Sunday school. For next winter it was intended to form a Lads' Club for the Sunday school boys. The savings bank was in a satisfactory position, and last year there stood to their account the creditable sum of £125 7s. 10d. The Brotherly Fund had been of considerable service, and they wanted to make the book scheme an educational concern. Mr. Cook seconded all that the Chairman had said in respect to missionary enterprise. The Church which was not missionary was not a living Church and they ought not to keep the good news to themselves. (Applause.).

div.head: LOCAL TEA PARTIES.
div.p: LOCAL TEA PARTIES.
ST. PETER'S CHURCH.

A very enjoyable gathering was the annual congrega- tional tea party in connection with St. Peter's Church, which was held in the schoolroom, John-street, on Monday evening. About 100 sat down to a good repast. After tea the Rev. B. Percival (vicar) presided, and said he was sorry that the Chruchwa rdens (Messrs. Bamforth and Steel) were unable to be present. He was pleased to inform them that St. Peter's parish bad subscribed a little over £35 17s. to the Church Pastoral kid Society during the past year, and he considered that a hand- some sum in the circumstances. (Applause Since the secietv was commenced, St. Peter's had contributed £3OO, and had received in return £1,500. (Applause.) An excellent entertainment was provided, and all the artistes acquitted themselves with great credit. Mrs. Sephton gave a pleasing interpretation of " A May morning," while Mr. E. Morris quite merited the lapplause he received for his rendering of " Peg away " and "Nuggets." Miss Violet Brown and Master Jack Greaves also gave several songs, and for the duet " Excelsior " they were warmly applauded. Mr. and Mrs. Sephton received a well-deserved encore for their rendering of " I beard a voice in the tranquil night." Master Young caused much amusement with his coon songs and stump speeches, and Miss B. Forshaw gave a I couple of recitations with good effect. Miss NI. Stanley maintained her reputation as a first-class mandoline player, and she was twice encored. The humorist was Mr. Shelly, who created great mirth with his songs. The accompaniments were played by Mr. F. Webster and Mr. Stanley. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Chair- man and to all who had helped to make the entertain. ment a success.

div.head: ST. JAMES', LATCFIFORD.
div.p: ST. JAMES', LATCFIFORD.

Success attended the annual congregational tea party in connection with St. James' Church which was held in the Schoolroom on Monday evening. About 300 parishioners and others sat down to tea, which was followed by a concert over which the Vicar (the Rev. H. B. Firth) presided. The assistant curate (the Rev. H. H. Corsbie) was among those present. The whole of the musical part of the programme was sustained by the Warrington Male Voice Choir, com- posed of 30 voices under the conductorship of Mr. Hassell, with Mr. J. Foster as accompanist. The choir fully maintained its reputation, the choruses being given with precision and musicianly taste. Particularly effective were "The Destruction of Gaza," " John Barleycorn," and "Phantom host." Songs were well rendered by Messrs. Clay and Hannan, and the quartettes" Simple Simon," and " The catastrophe were very pleasing items. A duet was also sung, and the performance throughout was most enjoyable. During an interval in the programme. The VICAR delivered a speech, in which he reviewed the work of the parish during the past twelve months. Having made a sympathetic reference to the illness of Mr. H. N. Houghton he referred to the changes which had taken place both in the congregation and in the church fabric. Churches, like human being., were liable to the ravages of time, and St. James' had shown Isigns of being prematurely old. But the decay had been ' arrested and the west end of the church made perfectly safe, and they could congratulate themselves upon having a church the interior of which wan in a very satisfactory condition,being both warm and comfortable. (Hear, hear and applause.) After a reference to several slight improvements which might be carried out during the year, the Vicar said that what he wanted to speak about more particularly was the clergy staff. At present there were two clergymen in the parish which contained 7,500 people, and those who had made a study of the needs of parishes contended that there ought to be one clergyman for every 2,000 people. Therefore they required another clergyman in that parish, and he was pleased to tell them that he had procured the services of another colleague, who hoped to he ordained in ,Tune. He would, he expected, come to them some- time about July. It was now necessary' that the Mission Church (St. Hilda) should be superseded by a more suitable building. They had a great respon- sibility in regard to that part of the parish which lay between Grove-street and Black Bear Bridge, because there was springing up quite a new town in that direction, and the Church of England ought to be properly represented by a handsome building. It was intended to hold a bazaar in that room in November to raise a fund, part of which would go to the cost of the erection of the new church and part serve as a reserve fund for defraying incidental expenses in con- nection with St. James' they would otherwise not be able to pay. (Applause.) After the concert dancing was kept up with spirit till 11.30.
CAIRO-STREET CHAPEL. REV. J. F. MATTHEWS' OPTIMISM.

Sunday witnessed the 237th anniversary of Cairo- street Chapel and eloquent. serMons were preached by the Rev. J. Colin-Odgers, of Liverpool. On Monday evening the annual congregational , ing was held in the school. Between ninety a._ hundred sat down to tea, ladies of the congregation presiding at the tables. A meeting followed, Mr. F. W. Monks occupying the.chair.

The CHAIRMAN said that in days gone by that con- gregation had taken an active part in various kinds of work, but he was sorry to say that from various causes, principally, he believed, due to deaths and with- drawals, they were not at present doing as much as was formerly done or as ought to be done. He urged them to consider whether they could not do better in the future, and try to promote more missionary enterprise. They had a faith, and it seemed to be a necessary corollary that they should give ether people the benefit of it. He would like them to take an active step that would not only influence others but do good to themselves—something that would promote A feeling of enthusiasm end help forward the aims and objects they had before them. There was cause for gratification in the excellent way the Sunday school was carried on, not only as regarded the classes, bvt the subsidiery organizations. Mr. J. S. HILL said the Sunday school was the brightest spot in their work, and he did not think they ever had a better band of workers then they now bad. They all appreciated Miss Bancroft's twenty-five years' services, and it WAS intended shortly to recognize her work in some tangible form. Mr. D. PLINsTON, in reviea ine, the work of the school organizations, said there had been a slight decrease in the attendance at Sund ty school, but he hoped they would make up the deficiency during the present year and establish record figures. The average attendance in the morning was 83, and in the afternoon 147. All the various institutions were in a flourishing condition, and it was worthy of note that through the book club 120 books had been distributed. The CHAIRMAN explained that it was arraneed that the Rev. J. Colin-Odgers should address them that evening. hut he was prevented through the sudden death of Mr. C. W. Jones, of Liverpool. whose funeral took place that day. He thought the Unitarian body during the last ten or twelve years had more to thank Mr. Jones for than any other member. He was a most generous man, always in the forefront of every good work, and he had been the means of raising more money in Liverpool and throughout the country for various Unitarian institutions than any other men. The Rev I J. F. Matthews had kindly stepped into the breach caused by Mr. Collin-Odgers' absence, and he was too well known to need introduction. The Rev. J. F'. MaTTREws said he had more than 'ordinary pleasure in being present. There was a kind I of homeliness at Cairo-street which reminded him very much of the homeliness of his own church at Latchford and to a visitor from another ecclesiastical communion it was an extraordinary advantage to come to an atmos- phere so congenial. if they had a Mohammedan Mosque, a Hindoo temple and a Jewish synagogue in their midst, he would he thankful fi he were asked by the people associated with those places to go amongst them. He would not go because of any specious breadth of view or extraordinary sympathy that other people did not possess, but because as a religious man the predominant feeling in one's heart was absolute kinship with the whole of humanity. (Applause.) He did not minimise their ecclesiastical differences. 'rhey we-e incidental to their life. They differed because they thought, and because they lived. It was right they should differ, and he did not deprecate the existence/of ,reeds. They had their value—their neces- sary valne. They were, intellectually and historically, landmarks.So long as men intellectual ised about God and human experience and the relation of the human to the , infinite, they were bound to have some sort of theology. and it was inevitable they should have creeds, but the trouble had been in the past that they had demanded that a man should adhere to a certain creed before his pulpit efficiency was certified—that he should believe in a certain formula before he was admitted to Church fellowship. in these days they did not stand so much for a form of creed as a life that was sweet and bright and wholesome and clean and good. He did not share in the lachrymose attitude and speeches made in con- nection with their congregational church life in these days. It did not bother him one hit that some of the churches were getting empty. He wished some of the pulpits would get empty. (Laughter.) Because the churches were getting empty it did not follow that Christianity was dying out. That the spirit and ethic that marked their Church life was in the aseendant was only too obvious, and it was growinglv in the ascendant too. Be was not at all astonished that Mr. Ramsay Macdonald in his new book on Socialism had taken up the wicked and stupid challenge thrown out by people who wanted to injure Socialism, that they were mainly Atheists. Mr. Macdonald said that the prominent leaders of the Labour movement to-day were grown on Free Church soil. They learned their powers of debate in Free Church debating societies, and Warrington had during he last hundred years turned out men of ability stut power. it would be a disgrace to Cairo- treet if it did not continue to grow voting men who took a conspicnous place not only in Free Church life but in public polity and municipal life as well. He wished to call attention to two elements in their common Christianity. The first was its splendid optimism. They of all men could afford to be the most buoyant, hopeful and optimistic. It was not an optimism that neglected the facts of life, that igeored the tragedies of life, that refused to face the great mystery of pain and is tiering. Some of `hem were compelled to carry the

div.head: Bold Farmer's Capture.
div.p: Bold Farmer's Capture.

A singular story was told at St. Helens County Pett Sessions, on Tuesday, when a man who gave the namk of Walter Smith, was charged with breaking into the dwelling-house of Thomas Smith, farmer, of Union Bank Farm, Bold. Superintendent Basendale said the man was known as Walter Noble, and by other names. About one o'clock on the morning of the 17th inst.,Mrs. Smith heard some noise, and awakened her husband,. He listened for a short time, and came to the conclu- sion that someone was breaking into the house. They got up and went to the top of the staircase and could see the figure of a man actually breaking into the hall window. Mr. Smith dressed and dropped out of the bedroom window at the back of the house and

quietly round to the front, armed with a poker. Ht saw Smith breaking open the window with a screvr=l driver. He spoke to the man and struck him on thel top of the head with a poker. The man tried to rnn. away, but on receiving two or three blows over the body, he aaid, "I am properly caught ; I will give in." Mr, Smith then made him pull everything out of hie pockets, and he found Smith was wearing a gold watch and chain, with a spade guinea. attached, and he had a long silver watchguard, two screwdrivers, a bicycle lamp, a razor, and a knife. By his side he had a can, which was identified as belonging to Mr. Smith's brother.

Police-constable Carson spoke to receiving prisoner from the custody of Mr. Smith at Prescot in the eady morning. lie charged .prisoner with attempting to break into his house, when Smith said he had nothing to say. He produced some of the articles found 0; prisoner, but Superintendent Baxendale said that th watch aol the two chains had been identified as belong-, ina to a farmer near Chester, whose house was broken', into on December 27th.

The second chxrge of breaking into the house of Nfr. George Smith, Cranshaw flail. Bold, and stealing tho can ems then gono into. Evidence showed that some- one had broken into the back kitchen window and helped himself to food, consisting of lib. of beef - ball' a loaf.
Accused was committed to the Assi.:cs, on both charges.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Modern Princess.—Twentieth century princesses fully share in the great liberty that is now customarily accorded to unmarried girls, and whilst the Duke and Duchess of Connaught have taken up their residence in Malta, Princess Patricia hns gone on a two months' visit to her sister, the Crown Princess of Sweden. 'Queen Victoria would have been horrified at the idea of her daughters going on their own account upon holiday tours, paying country house visits, and doing much as they liked, and with exceptions on very rare occasions, she was never separated from her daughters until they became brides. Such ideas have passed with the Victorian period, and the change is equally marked in all classes of Society. Princess Patricia is attended by the Hon. Lady Egerton, and her presence is very welcome at, the Court at Stockholm. Owing to delicate health the Queen of Sweden always winters in the Mediterranean, and the companionship of her sister will be of great assistance to the Crown Princess. who has thus an important part to play as a royal hostess. The London and Paris Dress Exhibition.—Women of fashion have been much interested in the Dress Exhibition at Earl's Court, in London, which remains open for two weeks only, and closes on February 6th. Tt has been promoted in a spirit of friendly rivalry between the leading houses of London and Paris, and about one hundred girls appear displaying the latest and most gorgeous triumphs of the dressmakers' and milliners' arts. Some interesting tableaux are also presented each day, including scenes in the life of the ultra fashionable woman, and the ideal gown for such occasions, such as a dress for the fashionable dinner Party • a meet of hounds ; an up-river picnic ; and so en. it is chiefly an exhibition of how extravagantly a woman can be dressed, but it is an interesting display even to those who have to study economies of dress and are not in the inside circle of the world of fashion. The show is no exception to the rule nowadays, that prizes are the leading feature of every enterprise, and to the best dressed woman who visits the exhibition a twenty-five guinea evening gown will he presented, and a ten guinea hat to the one wearing the smartest head- gear. A Useful Exhibitien.—To Mrs. Charles Muller helenes the credit of organizing 'a very practical and useful exhibition, which is to be held at Princes Skating Rink in London in May. It is he called " What to do with our Girls Exhibition," and is intended, as its title implies, to show in actual operation, every trade, profession, or calling, at which educated girls can, and do, earn money. It may thus afford to numbers of parents and girls useful ideas for the solution of a knotty problems ns it will not only show in actual working such occnpa- ' as book-binding, glass-blowing, enamelling, .Ig, and so on, but will afford information as to 1)--e-c "Inching, training. and qualifications necessnry to pr come proficient in these callings and the possible fmcl 81;"'"able income that may he derived from them. In .„,. • nearly a hundred different occupations will be 'uown in operation, and it is obvious that this will !serve a very useful purpose in providing informanion `mll ideas as to the various careers open to girls. A Favourablerhance for Government Clerkships.— Girls who have been preparing for the Civil Service will have an unusually favourable chance of securing an anpointrnent at the next examinations, which takes Place on Februnry 18th. /tiers women instead of men clerks are to be employed in the Savings Bank Depart- ment, and there are no fewer than 200 vacancies for girls from 18 to 20 years of age. Positions in the Savings Bank Department are among the most desirable of all the branches of the Civil Service open to women, and there being many more vacancies than usual, candi- dates have a much better chance of successfully passing the examinations Two languages out of three—French, aermass, Latin,—nre compulsory, and other subjects include shorthand and mathematics. A special course of teaching, with more or less " cramming," is neces- sary to secure a reasonable chance of successfully pnasing the stiff examinations. , The Makin of Gold and Precious Stones.—We are nearing 9 good deal jest now and then of some dis- covery that may have some hearing upon the trans- rnatation of metals, but there was an old law passed in b the time of Henry IV., probably still in force, which ' Prohibits the making of gold or precious stones,becanse of the ruin it would bring upon those in possession of "Ch treasures. That however did not prevent the old . seekers after the philosopher's stone, from continuing their search, of their experiments, and in fact several . of Henry TV's successors listened to the tales of the • alehemists in the hope of establishing a monopoly in Ilhe making of gold, wherewith to pay their debts and Ov° high old times. Bet, Queen Elizabeth said that Walter Raleigh was the only man who really turned ,n. 'laser element into gold. He laid her a wager that he ij,:ld weigh the smoke from his pipe, which she sPliPht. impossible. She however paid her debt when , 'r Waite solved the problem by weighing first the tol, r 'aPeo and then the ashes, the difference he said, was ~,- tha • .eleht of the smoke. .i The New Coiffure.—The latest notion in hairdressing cnn scarcely be ronsidsred an improvement upon quite 1 recent modes. It consists of many heavy " sausage " rolls Pinned at both ends, and grouped sometimes all , ever the head in such a way as to afford a curiously ..: wide and flat appearance, at others, at the back only, chignon fashion. The effect is heavy, and certainly not ; becoreing, and we can only hope that the very np-to- ; date will quickly tire of the idea. As regards colour, that is acquired colour, brown without any suggestion iv of gold, soft, silky, light brown,more akin to pale °tide t than to gold, has fashion's enthusiastic approval for .the moment. It is an expensive colour, and one only the most skilful manipulation can prodoce. Sleeves and No Sleeves.—Although modistes are l. decidedly favouring the "no sleeve " fashion for , evening bodices, they are building a few with " Angel " draperies, generally for possessors of thin or red arms. Taken altogether, our arms are not our strong point, and it is a matter fcr regret that vast numbers of us cannot he persuaded to at any rate partially cover them up. But to return to the " Angel " draperies. 1. These are invariably of transparent material, and fall low under the arms. On the outer side they are open ' right up to the shoulder, but some ornament, such as a lone glittering insect or flower, is usually employed to hold the fragile material together just above the elbow. ' Infinitely flattering, and particularly artistic are these tt . Angel " draperies. Bead Trimmings upon Velvets.-'-Beautiful shot velvets have made their appearance nod are being 11‘,Xtensirelv utilised for early spring toilettes. So far Lay have been employed more in the form of trimmings "P.en cloth or homespun but entire little coats built °I these shot velvets will shortly be in evidence. Very !mart little additions to a dressy toilette too, will Prove the plain velvet wraps, ornamented with head • triMmings, that are just now hailing from Paris. Of • course there is always present the danger of overdoing the bead trimming, but really good tailors and dress- Makers are not likely to err in this direction. ,The Reformed London Cab.—Commencing in F ebruary, London's horse-drawn cabs are to be fitted .I;_ith taximeters. The fare for the hansom-cab will ' 'nen he sixpence for the first mile and threepence for eh additional half-mile. This is a little lower than 'lle charge for the taximeter motor-cab, which however seems likely to supersede the older vehicles. It has .„rn,anY advantages. The journey is accomplished in a Shorter time, and there is no question of cruelty to over-driven cab-horses. Another advantage of the reformed London cab is that the passenger is relieved from the extortion and abuse which formerly prevented

A very fascinating tailor-made costume of Parisian design and English make is in rough tweed, narrowly striped with golden brown and dull old rose. The pleats of the skirt are stitched down to the knee, and the hem, which clears the ground, is ornamented with several undulat- ing lines formed of pipings covered with the %weed and stitched with pink silk. The coat is cut to come below the waist, but without a basque. It is bound with brown silk braid, and has revers of brown velvet and a smart waistcoat of smooth brown cloth, fastening with pink enamel buttons, and lined with pink silk. To go with this there is a smart little brown hat made of felt and trimmed with pink and brown mara- bout. There is also a more severe little toque in brown felt with two brown knife-feathers with pink stems.

There was also a strap of the plain-coloured flannel over each shoulder, finished with a velvet button at the points. The sleeves • were a plain bishop shape, and drawn into pointed cuffs trimmed with velvet buttons. THE TAINT OF CRUELTY.

The terrible, and now famous, York cruelty case makes us pause, writes "Lady Phyllis" in the Bystander, to wonder whether, as a nation, we can really boast of the humanitarian prin- ciples our civilisation professes. Now and again the better and educated classes have given us an instance of a brutality we should not expect to find in the lowest, while the lowest grade of Eng- lish society could scarcely resent it as unjust if, after drunkenness, we described cruelty to chil- dren as its national sin, the "black stain" of our cities, and even villages. Our country knows such extremes on the subject, and side by side with the child tyrant, petted, fussed over, in- dulged as the children of no other race. is the child tyrannised, treated with a brutality and neglect surely possible to no other civilised people. It is a matter for surprise that the great Society which is doing such excellent work in the direction of checking the evil is ignored by a large number of people with children of their own to whom the object should be dear. It would not be too great an honour to pay if all well-to-do parents banded their children together to assist its work, and -ncf-our those unfortunate ones needing its protection. CARE OF OSTRICH PIX:IES.

Keeping ostrich plumes from one season to .inother is quite a. .serious question, for when. *id away flat in a box or rolled in tissue paper, means that the spring will fitid it a very sorry- looking plume, with the strands mangy -look- ing or twisted entirely out of shape, so that re- curling becomes an urgent necessity. To keep feathers in their original shape, and in the best condition, says our Paris correspondent, they should be ripped from the hat and pinned securely by the wired end to one side of a small box, and this can be weighted to keep it from being overbalanced by the plumo. Several feathers can be pinned upright around the one box, and this can be placed in a hat-box tall enough not to bend the feathers, tops down, a lump of camphor also put in, and the box tied up and stowed away.

div.head: "LAWYERS AND THE LAW." Mr. E. England's Paper to the
div.p: "LAWYERS AND THE LAW." Mr. E. England's Paper to the
Jailor Liberals.

Lawyers and the law" was the subject of a chatty -nd interesting paper given by Mr. E. England at the meeting of the Junior Literal Association held at Gregory's Cafe on Monday evening. He showed how the ideas of the public Kith regard to the lawyers had changed, for whereas lawyers at one time were con- sidered to be not only authorities on law, but on almost every question of life as well, the community, thanks to the great progress of education, had now got an idea that they could teach the lawyer a little, and were some- times actually not afraid to do without him even in legal matters. The latter course, however, was not always wise. There was a prevailing notion that mem- bers of the legal profession thought of themselves first and their clients last, though be had no hesitation in saying that the notion was somewhat erroneous. As a proof of that he might stato that there were more actions settled out of Court by the advice of the lawyers than in Court by the decision of the judges. Of course there were lawyers who did advise "fighting" on almost every possible occasion in order to run up a bill of costs for themselves, but, happily, they were in the minority. In the good old times, as they were often miscalled, there were some curious laws—among the Anglo baxons (our ancestors) every portion of the body had a .recognised monetary value and anyone injuring the person of another had to pay his victim the legal price of the damage done. To-day in the present state of the law they could not gauge what one would receive in case of an accident RS it was left to a Judge and twelve "good men and true," generally termed a "jury," to assess the damages. In addition the status or social position of tbe victim was taken into consideration and it was astonishing to see the different values which were put upon the people. If the plaintiff was a workman he most not expect much and be not dis- appointed, but if be moved in what is termed the 1" higher circles" he would expect to receive some- where about four figures. The law was incongrous on that point—or rather the courts assessed wrongly— because undoubtedly it was the poor man who needed the money whereas the rich man has it and could do without the heavy damages. Surely the limbs and bodies of everyone of us were of equal value and there should be no distinction. One would imagine that in this so-called enlightened twentieth century our laws would be well nigh perfect. But it was remarkable when one came to look at the Statute Books and knew what the present jaws were, to find what ridiculous and absurd laws were still in force. Mr. England then gave instances of the anomalies of the Inheritance and Divorce Laws. One of the greatest. evils of the egat system, he said, was the expense connected with it. A great portion of the public were prevented from seeking its aid and protection in con- sequence of the costs they would incur. Our land laws' continued Mr. England, were a disgrace to our vaunted civilization and intelligence of the twentieth century. The land, which was undoubtedly the chief element for our existence, was allowed to be bartered for, and even leased or sold to the highest bidder. In other words, wealth only was allowed to have the control of it. It wee acknowledged after several thousands of years' trial that private ownership of land was one vast curse and abet the sooner it was merged into the hands or control of the State the better it would be for the welfare of the whole com- munity. What the people wanted were :—laws which an average person could understand ; laws which would facilitate the transacting of business instead of causing delay: laws which would simplify the transferring of property from one person to another at such a cost as would not be a burden upon the seller and purchaser; laws which would treat all sections of the community alike so that there would be no privileged class. (Applause.) ' Councillor 3. HAWTHORN (who presided) moved a vote of thanks to Mr. England for his admirable address and expressed the hope that they had derived a great deal of benefit f rem it. Mr. H. W. DI:EST seconded and the motion was carried unanimously.

Collecting from a letter box in Oaklands, Breconshire, this week a postboy found no correspondence to collect but there was a half-sovereign in the box, hid) the , ad handed in at the post office in the usual way.

div.head: ORDEAL OF MYLES ROTHERHAM.
div.p: ORDEAL OF MYLES ROTHERHAM.
BY CHRISTIAN LYS,
Luthor of "The Fortress of Yadasara," "The Hepworth Millions," "The Mystery of Lady- place," "The Opening Door." ecc.

..cit .a-Tte him witrn•rni; "Should I zet' ter. von use this against , me," he said ; "t.t. do ettt think lam likely to ; get better. If I ti.i hOlad still.)). too much of a co.,.iird he truth. Mollie ' von must tell the vicat• till he does not understand. II Perhaps you will r ;ail it n -ett,er presently." Mollie sat on the edge of the bed and took the thin band in hers. "It was I who killed teeter Fenton.' "Father!" "That night when I eni-th home to you and made my promise, I had just 1.1.. bite, left him as you found him next day. We had quarrelled that afternoon—indeed, we had quarrelled a good deal about that time. chiefly over money matters in : which he was swirthilinir nth. lam not excusing elvselr. I was not sol.er and I was badly in need : of money just then, and went that night to got some out of Fenton. As I 'sent op to the door of the house it opened, and Myles Rotherham cams oat. With a brief nod I passed him and went her No one but Myles Rotherham saw me enter, no one at all saw me leave. I locked Fenton's door . afterwards and dropped the key into the area." "Father ! Surely, surely-- " "I was a coward. I let Myles Rotherham suffer for my crime. He could have spoken. He must. have guessed the truth, but something kept him silent. I think I know what it was." "It cannot be trite I It cannot be true!" sobbed Mollie. "Even now the door opens through which I must pass to my Judge," said Templeton, solemnly. "You must let the truth be known at once. Do not wait fur my going." "Father! Father!" "Alt, Mollie, if only I had had the courage to speak before!" The vicar touched the girl gently on the shoulder. "Leave us a little while, my child," he said. "I will come to you later." She bent down and kissed her father's face. "Come and sit with me presently, Mollie," he whispered. Then 81th left the room. It could not be true. Her father a murderer! ; And then her t houghts flew to that other, working out I his punishment for a crime he had never committed. , What had kept him silent? The look in his face when their eyes had met that terrible day, had I burnt into her soul. She had hated the crime, yet ; had pitied the criminal. Now she understood. It , was for her sake he had not spoken. What could she say to her father when she went I to sit with him presently ? What comfort could she give ? The vicar had gone until to-morrow. He would come and read the confession with her then, he said. The doctor had come, and Mollie sat holding her father's hand in hers. That was his comfort; he needed nothing more, no spoken sympathy. / Once he looked at her and smiled, then his eyes closed. His fingers gradually tightened upon l hers, and so evening came, and the stars over the quiet land; and into the night—death's night—a soul drifted, drifted, and was lost in the far dimness. Doubtless there were expectant hands stretched out to take it yonder, and if human hands were kind and human hearts forgiving, who dare think that the Hands yonder, and If treat Heart yonder were less merciful?

. . . . . • In her garden Mollie lingered, though the day was done. k shawl Was wrapped closely round her, for it was cold. Half-a-dozen times had the old servant been to beg her to go in, yet still she waited by the gate. There was a late carrier from the market town that night, and she could not go in until he had gone. He had not yet passed to the village. She would have heard the grind of the wheels at the end of the lane. The letter—it was still in her pocket—had said: "May I come ?" And her brief answer had been: "Come I "
There came a low sound from the distance, growing sharper. Then the barking of a dog. Then wheels grinding, grinding. A pause, a hasty "Good-night," then the wheels go grinding on again. . . . _

Footsteps in the lane—quick footsteps. Then for the first time Mollie was afraid. How might not this terrible ordeal have changed hint Was it not her father who had made him suffer it? How should she meet him? What could she say? A quick step, and then a hand upon the gate, falling upon hers. " Mollie I" "Myles!"
Then a long, long silence. She took his hand and led him gently towards the cottage. "I want to see you plainly,' she said. "Come into the light." . .
He bent-d.urn to her. "Mollie, my dearest, let us go quickly into the light—together."
[Tint Est), 1

div.head: OIL EXTRACTION.
div.p: OIL EXTRACTION.
Question of a Secret Process.

In the Lancashire Chancery Court at Liverpool on Monday, Vice-Chancellor Leigh Clare had before him a motion by Messrs. Silcock and Sons, of Liverpool, feeding cake and bone manure manufacturers, to restrain Edward Stephenson, an oil extractor and refiner, from committing a breach of agreement of September, 1905. It appeared that Stephenson, who possessed a secret process for extracting oil from seeds by chemical means, entered plaintiff's employ for the purpose of superintending the adaptation of certain buildings and machinery to the work of oil extraction by such secret process. They agreed to pay him a capital sum of £2OO in addition to a weekly wage, and he covenanted that on ceasing to work for them, he should not for ten years, be concerned in oil extraction work in any place within thirty miles of Liverpool, Bristol, or London. lie left plaintiff's employ towards the end of last year, and they now complained that for several weeks past he had been working for one of their competitors, Messrs. Crosfleld, at Warrington. Stephenson denied by affidavit that he was at present doing or intended to do anything having to do with oil extraction in connection with Messrs. Crosfield's machinery, and also contended that the scope of the agreement was too wide. His Honour granted an injunction pending trial of the motion.

It must be admitted THE PROMISE that the new Session of OF THE Parliament did not make a SESSION. distinguished commence.

ment. The House of Commons rose before half-past nine o'clock, and, of course, the House of Lords rose some hours earlier. To the ordinary observer, such events as these are disappointing. The public exoeetation is that, after many months of rest, Parliament will open out on what, in reference to one of our chief industries, is called " full blast." As a matter of fact, this impetuous proceeding to work is something that never happens. There are assiduous members of Parliament who sit up all night in order to gain a privileged seat. Taey are the objects of national admiration—or amazement. But when the House of Commons actually meets on the first day of the Session, it is in a condition of lassitude. It is willing to listen to the speeches of the proposer and seconder of the Address to the Throne, however uninteresting they may be; but after these have been heard it wants its dinner and goes in search for it—which is why the P arils- rnentary proceedings came to so early a close on Wednesday night. The KING'S Speech will awaken feelings that are precisely in conflict with each other. It will go too far for some members of the Liberal party who have been affrighted by the hypocritical cry about Socialism, and not far enough for others, who, nevertheless, do not wish to approach Socialism. It is a practical Speeah, dealing with actual problems of Statesmanship in a Statesman- like manner. What are the measures that are to be placed in the forefront of the Government pro- gramme ? Oa the financial side, Old Age Pensions take the fiest place. The proposals to be made on this subject will, of course, be as part of the Budget. The views of the House of Lords do not count in this case. What- ever Mr. AsQUITII may have determined upon doing will really be done if his scheme should be accepted by the House of Commons. The Licensing Bill, however, is to be the chief Bill of the Session. It is placed in front of everything else in his Alajesty's Speech. We are all by thit time fairly acquainted with the character of this measure. The" Trade" is pretending that it is to be robbed of something like one hundred millions of what it considers to be its proprietary interest in the liquor traffic, But we have yet to learn that there are to be any " spoliation" proposals. What we do know is that the proposals of the Govern- ment will not convert a license for a year into a perpetual monopoly. The object of the Licensing Bill will be, in the first place, to give to the people some real control over licenses, and to ,recover that popular influence over licenses which was given away by Mr. Bkr..Foue.'s ridiculous and unjust measure. The Education Bill is the second—perhaps it ought to have been the first—measure in the Government programme. It will, of course, be the measure most hotly opposed, though it has the strongest pressure of public opinion behind it. We should be too sanguine if we expected the E iucation question to be eettled in the present Session of Parliament. It will probably not be settled until . the House of Lords question has been settled once and for all. In the next few weeks, however, it will be presented in its simplest, and what will probably be the final form, until the conflict with the House of Lords is absolutely brought to ail end by the recognition on the part of that Assembly that it has of late been claiming powers to which the Constitution, written or unwritten, gives it no right whatever. The other measures proposed in the Kusn's Speech are such as will command the general assent of all persons who are not reactionaries in politics. The Speech is the presentation of a great and most reasonable political programme. Any objection to it can only

arise from those who want too much or those who believe that too much is being offered. The Liberal patty must always, of course, lose support from either one or another of these causes. Bit, whatever happens, it must abide by its principles and its aims.

Warrington Bridge has not WARRINGTON quite become a standing BRIDGE. joke, but it might easily descend to such a level were it not for the fact that its daily congested I state constitutes a public danger and nuisance. For years now the Corporation has tried to remedy I the difficulty and failed. Oae would have thought that to a Corporation unanimous on the point the matter would have been simpler. Bat ic took a long time to get the Council to on 3 way of thinking. Eventually they decided upon widening by cantilevers—an economical and adequate scheme. Tney let the contract, and the contractor bored some preparatory holes in the mud at the base of the pillars. Apparently the work had commenced. Then it ceased very soddenly and since then the Corporation seems to hawo found the Mersey Conservator some- what of a stumbling block, and even now the plans have not received his sanction. Bit the biggest obstructionists to the widening scheme have all along been Messrs. J. Fairclough and Sons, Limited. They insist upon a new bridge for selfish reasons, and we are not surprised that the Mayor voiced some of the municipal resent- ment in the course of a colloquy with Mr. 8,. T. Fairclough at the Chamber of Commerce on Thursday. He said bluntly that the cantilever scheme would have been carried out by now but for the Fairzlough opposition, and in spirited tdhes he added that " the Corporation was not going to be dictated to by three people when there were 70,000 people to consider." The Bridges Sub-Committee report that they met Messrs. Fairclough on January 97,11 in order to confer with them about the cantilever scheme, but that the representatives of the firm " peremptorily refused to consider the plans." Tnis is the sort of 1 attitude they have adopted all along. A new bridge or no alteration is apparently their ultiinatum. We hope the Mayor and Corporation I will stiffen their backs and carry out this most urgent improvement despite opposition which seems to be dictated by anything but a commend- able spirit..

Warrington's one municipal BOWLING GREENS. bowling green is soon to have company if Councillor Pemberton's persistence is rewarded. He his long been tilting at the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee for their slowness in extending the facilities for municipal bowls, and on Tuesday be will take the drastic step of proposing resolu- tions in the Council Chamber for no less than five new greens to be laid down at once arid opened in the coming summer. Cauncillor Pemberton has two resolutions respeoting Victoria Park, one apparently depending upon the other. The first authorises two new greens in addition to the one already there, and the second suggests the provision of only one addi- tional green. The other resolutions provide for greens in Orford-lane, St. Elphin's Park, and Sankey Recreation Grounds. If Councillor Pemberton only gets two of his five resolutions through he will have reason to be satisfied. The popularity of the experimental greea at Victoria Park, Latchford, has been such as to scatter all the old arguments which were used in opposition to the original scheme. We were told then " that grass would not grow in Warrington," but it grows as quickly as the busy feet of the bowlers will let it. The extension of municipal facilities for recreation of this kind is worthy of warm advocacy and we hope a substantial part of Councillor Peinberton's scheme will be heartily supported.

There was a good repro- SEC )ND.ARY sentation of the Education EDUCATION. Committee at Wednesday evening's meeting of the Shorthand Writers' Association, when " Higher Education" was under consideration, and Mr. G. J. Brown, the popular President, took the oppor- tunity of saying a few words in season. Tie particular point on which he criticised the action of the Committee was the institu tion of compulsory courses of study at the Technical Institute. This means that a student canna select the subject which he particularly requires in his work but must take two others— " allied " subjects they are termed, but in the case of the commercial course Mr. Brown said they 11 were as wide apart as the poles. He did not I hesitate to predict that that course, at any rate, would be a failure. Wa 13hal! be rather surprised if it is not. Toe Cominittse have shown a great want of consideration for the student whose time for study is very limited but , who is anxious to increase his store of knowledge in some special department. To many it is an utter impossibility to take up three subjects seriously and do the necessary home work, and we are pleased to hear from the Principal that the system will probably undergo revision next year. The Cmnrnittee should bear in mind that the primary object of such classes should be to render the greatest possible service to the rising genera- tion and this cannot be attained by laying down burdensome rules which in a great number of cases cannot be complied with.
Lord Barton, Mr. Samuel CANDID BREWEELS. Whitbread, and Mr. Waters

Butler (chairman of the Brewers' Society) have issued a manifesto against the" time limit" advocated by the Temperance Legislation League and by the Church of Eogland Temperance Society. In some ways this document is more frank than others emanating from the same source. A clearer statement of the root of the difficulty than this, for example, could not be wished: e -rras

The existing licensed houses, being in posses- sion of a practical monopoly, have acquired a very high value. Taking tnree of the oldest brewing companies in London, the writers of the circular have probably good grounds for their estimate that out of the £10,160,692 worth of licensed houses which they own, no less than £7,000,000 is pure monopoly, in excess of the value of site, buildings and fittings, and therefore a free gift from the State to those companies. The point at issue is the nature of tho right to the monopoly value created by a licence. Previous to 1904, as is admitted by the signatories, the licence was only an annual grant, there was no right to renewal, but only an "expec- tation of renewal," and it was this "expectation which acquired the enormous market value which it now has. Bat the brewers talk as if this " expectation '' were-a freehold, and as if they had a right to complain if the expectation were not fulfilled. Tney forget that even since 1901 that monopoly value is very far from being a freehold. It is always liable to be depreciated, if not destroyed, by the creation of fresh and competing licences in the neighbourhood. It is liable to compensation levies in order to extinguish neigh- bouring licences. It is liable to heavier and more adequate licence duties. As a matter of fact, a monopoly value loased only upon an expectation and subject to such qualifications is merely an investment of the most speculative order.

On Monday the compensation authority for London awarded a surn of £1.08,653 for the extinction of thirty-eight licences in different parts of ' the metropolis. The extent to which compensation has been paid and licences reduced in London and other towns adds to the complexity of the problem with which the Government has to deal. AU those whose licences have been extinguished have received their full compensation value, but if a time limit is proposed and the provision of the Act of 1901 altered, the whole position will be changed and licences may be with- drawn without any compensation whatever.

A Sub-committee of the Pinata2e Committee requasts the Town Hall Committee to instruct the Borough Surveyor to prepare plans and estimates for an extension at both ends of the Town Hall to accommo- date all the departments of the Corporation. This is a step towards the long-looked hr centialisation of municipal offices which we hope will be rapidly followed by others. _ .

* * * Mr. Wilmot Lunt, the well-known local artist, con- tributes a smart sketch to this week's " London Opinion." It illstrates the following joke : Kindly Old Soul: "And how do you know,my little man, that you have been christened ? " Tommy Trattles : " Please, mum, 'cause I got the marks on me arm now, mum !

The Warrington :Garden Suburbs project has advanced another stage Plans for the laying out of the Great Sankey and Grappenhall estates have been accepted and all the designs sent in —2l in number— will be on view at the Old Academy until 9.30 this evening. We would advise the public to take advantage of this opportunity of judging for them- selves as to the possibilities of the scheme. They will, we have no doubt, be go favourably impressed that they will at once decide to become practical supporters. * * * Ths Warrington Chamber of Commerce keeps pegging away at the Warringtan lay-by question but it cannot be said that great progress has been made in this direction during the past year. A proper approach has been made to the lay-by, electric light installed, and a warehouse provided, but the most important feature —the regular stoppage of a line of steamers at Warrington —still remains in abeyance. If only some concession could be obtained on this point, the project could be given a fair trial and it might be seen whether the dream of Warrington as a port was at all capable of realization.

* * * Lord Curzon has taken his seat in the House of Lords, and in a somewhat ambiguous note the Westminster Gazette " says :—" For our part, we are glad that Lord Curzon is once again in Parlia- ment, though Ni'"e should have preferred to see him in the House of Commons. Wa are sorry considerations of health made that impossible." Why ? The sug- gestion is obvious, if unintentional, that there is a vast difference between the strenuousness of life in the Lords and in the Commons. A man might die of overwork in the latter and sleep undisturbed in the " other place." . .

* * * In "gentlemen," the community excuses the gentlemanly vices in consideration of their possessing the gentlemanly virtues. Politics is a class instrument ; whichever class obtains possession of it uses it for the discomfiture of the other. •

Few men reach fifty, without being grateful that they did not get the woman they wanted. The modern woman gives the husband the honey- moon, and takes the rest of the life for herself. The more we cultivate reason in woman the more unreasonable she becomes. * * When the new chairman of the Labour party first appeared in politics there were some of his old friends who did not recognise him by the name of Arthur Henderson. They bad known him as Arthur Heath, and remembered him particularly, because of the zeal he showed as a leader of a little band who conducted a Wesleyan mission at Arthur's Hall, Newcastle-on- Tyne. Meeting him in Manchester not long ago, one of them made some reference to this. " Oh, there is no mystery about it," he replied. "My mother remarried while I was still young, and the neighbours, not unnaturally, got into the way of calling me by my stepfather's name. I accepted it tacitly for a time, but on joining a trade society I was obliged to give my proper name. So I became Henderson once again." _ _ ** * _ . .

- Alderman Forshaw is to move at Tuesday's Council meeting " That a copy of the whole of the proceedings with reference ta Lawson's Contract, inquiry and arbitration be presented to Councillor Pemberton as a slight recognition of the great interest he took in the matter." 'We hope the resolution will be carried unanimously. Councillor Pemberton devoted the bulk of his energies for two or three years in unravelling the tangled skein of the water contract, and it is questionable whether the present satisfactory settlement would have brAen possible but for his labours. To present him with a complete copy of all the proceedings seems only a slight recognition, but it svill doubtless be appreciated by the recipient.

The Parliamentary Debating Society was launched with great eclat on Thursday evening. Mr. C. Plinston (Speaker) and Mr. W. Alason (Clerk) awed everybody by appearing clothed in flowing white wigs and impressive dignity. After the "King's Speech ' had been read the debatinc, waxed fast and furious, and there was plenty of evidence that the Governmont and Labour parties are strong in debating power. The Opposition was somewhat handicapped by cir- cumstances, but it was a sad confession of weakness to import Mr. J. H. Bottomley of Earlestown, in order to take up the cudgels on their behalf. Worse still; Mr. Bottomley got the worst of a duel vtith the Secre- tary for Ireland (Mr. Avvbery) who severely hammered the Opposition champion. There was a fine gather- ing of members (they number 200 already), the proceedings were animated, and the auguries for the future were of the brightest.

* * * A report presented to the Electricity Committee by the Borough Engineer, Mr. F. V. L. Mathias, does not hold out the slightest hope to the Tradesmen's Association, whose members have petitioned for a decrease in the charges for electric light. Mr. Matthias points out that the Department is only making " a reasonabre surplus," and pronounces against any reduction in the price of current because ,of the abnormally high price of coal and other commodities used in the electrical business. The engineer; also urges that the price in Warrington is comparatively low, but the absolute conviction among tradespeople is that electric light is very dear. It seems that if they want the new illuminant they must pay for it, but the earning power of the Electricity Department will be closely watched. Meanwhile the Gas Committee has the laugh ! * * * The Presidential address of Mr. G. Holman Kingdon to the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, a summary of which we publish in another column,is exceptionally interesting and will fully repay perusal. As the representative of the Chamber on the Education Committee Mr. Kingdon touched on several momentous topics, the most important being that of infantile mortality. There are signs that public opinion is 'awakening to the full significance of the appalling loss of child life which goes on year after year. As Mr. Kingdon said, our record in Warrington is nothing to boast about, for with a high infantile mortality little or nothing has been done in the way of preventive measures, and this is a glaring example of the need of the application of commercial ideas on the subject. Touching upon business affairs, Mr. Kingdon paid a happy tribute to Mr. Lloyd George's successful inter- vention in the railway dispute and in regard to trade generally he ventured the opinion that there was no need to be unduly pessimistic, although it was hardly likely that the rate of progress of the last few years could be maintained.

Some very striking figures as to the demand for small holdings were quoted by Lord Carrington at the National Liberal Club on Monday night, where he and Mr. Lewis Harcourt were entertained in honour of their work in passing the Small Holdings Act. That measure has been in operation for little more than three weeks, and this is what Lord Carrington is able to say at the end of that time: Applications had come in from forty-five counties, among thorn being applications received from Oxford for 10,000 acres, Wiltshire for 6,000, Worcester for 5,000, Huntingdon for 5,1)00, Cambridgeshire for 5,000, Gloucestershire for 4,000, Buckinghamshire for 3,600, and Hereford for 3,000. In these eight counties alone a total of over 41,000 acres, over 641 square miles, had been applied for by 2,715 applicants. Besides this, over 12,000 acres of Crown lands had been applied for. making a rough total of eighty-three square miles applied for for small holdings, or, in other words, a strip of land a mile broad stretching from Charing Cross to Salisbury Cathedral. This is a splendid beginning, and it should have conequences in a few years that will mean a revolu- tion in rural conditions. No more complete justifica- tion of the policy of the Act could be sought. * *

It would be well if the 'Labour party could decide what the resolution passed at Hull last week really means. Mr. Ramsay Macdonald says that it means i nothing, Mr. Victor Grayson that t means everything, while Mr. Hyndrnan, as an old and veteran leader of the Socialists. declares that by the resolution the Labour party na.iletl. the red (lag to the mast. No one (says the London Correspmdeut of the " Liver- pool Post and Ifercury)"takes seriously 'gr.llaedortald's

view that the resolution is a mere piece of verbiage. This is, of course, the saying of an astute wirepuller who sees that the resolution was inexpedient, and that the less said about it the better. Mr. Maddison, M.P.' makes a strong appeal to trades unionist members of the Labour party, and especially to Mr. Shackleton, to dissolve the alliance. He points out that of the total sum of £8,951 subscribed to the Parliamentary fund, only £lB9 came from the non-Socialist societies. Out of the funds seven members of the Labour party receive £1,400 a year, ,but Mr. Maddison should remember also that some of trades unions, notably the Amalgamated Society of Engineers, have gone over completely to Socialism. For the present I do not believe that there will be any rupture in the Labour party. Mr. Shackleton will not withdraw so long as it does not attempt to give effect to purely Socialistic principles in the House of Commons, and this in the circumstances the Indepen- dent Labour group will be too prudent to do—at least as long as Hr. Ramsay Macdonald is their chairman.

Sensational Suicide from Warrington Bridge. About 2 a.m. yesterday an unknown man jumped into the river at Warrington Bridge with the cry " I am tired of roaming about, and I don't want to live." P.C. Hughes saw the deed and threw a life-belt, and this failing to reach the man he went into the water after him. The body,however, completely disappeared. A juvenile ball in aid of the fund for providing a children's cot in the Infirmary extension will be held. at the Parr Hall on Thursday, the 13th inst. from 7 to 11 p.m. The effort is a most worthy one and will it is hoped, be the precursor of numerous under- takings by which the funds to provide more cots will, be raised. The arrangements are in the hands of a committee with Mr. J. El. Smethurst as lion. secretary. The price of the tickets is 3s. each (including refresh- ments) and spectators will be admitted to the gallery at a charge of (id. each. The guests will be received by the Mayor and Mayoress. One of tho most successful smoking'concerts hi the history of the Warrington Cycling Club was held at the Patten Arms Hotel on Thursday evening. One hundred members and friends were present, and the. proceedings were enjoyable in the highest degree. The programme was sustained in its entirety by Mr. Tom Anderson's party, of Oldham, consisting of Messrs. Tom Anderson, William Lawton, Frank Barker, W. F. Spencer, and Tom Hibbert, who delighted the audience with songs, recitations, duets, pianoforte solos, and recitations. The gathering was presided over by Mr. Fred Fieldhouse, captain of the club. At the close a cordial vote of thanks was passed to the artistes on the proposition of Mr. G. H. Smith (secretary), seconded by Mr. George Bowman ; and Messrs". Anderson and Spencer responded.

Messrs. Milling's Cashier Dead. We regret to record the death of Mr. Robert Lowe, cashier to Messrs. Henry Milling and Co.' Ltd. who passed away at his residence, Brantwood, Manchester- road, at 1-30 yesterday morning. The deceased gentleman, who was forty-eight years of age, had been suffering from lung trouble for a considerable time and had not been able to attend to business for several weeks. So recently as on Thurs- day morning, however, he paid a visit to the office and the news of his death yesterday came as a shock. Ho had been connected with the firm for thirty-four years, joining the office staff as a youth. The deceased gentleman who was greatly respected, leaves a widow, two daughters and a son with whom great sympathy is felt in their bereavement.
