Mr. Sydney -Carter's famous Yew Century pictures have again been the attraction at the Parr Hall this week. There is a complete change of programme and the audiences have been large and appreciative. One of the best pictures is ' Only a limerick." The humorous element as usual is well to the f )re " Her first bike ride " " Why the wedding was put off "and " Father buys a lawn roller" being particularly mirth provoking. There is a fine set of views illustrating life and scenes on the " Fiji islands " whilst the " Workingmans' Christmas " is a pathetic picture which appeals to all. A novel feature of the pro- gramme each evening has been a competition open to all Warrington for the best entertainer, the audience being the :judges. The competition has been taken up with considerable spirit and has afforded pleasure and amusement. This afternoon there will be a matinee and the concluding performance will be given this evening. - ---•-- For Perfection in BACON try ASHLEY'S.—Advt. Presentation to Miss Taylor. At a social held in the schoolroom of the St. Clement's Mission on Thursday night, a presentation was made to Miss Taylor, of Manchester-road, of a silver rose bowl by the members of the young ladies' Bible, class in recognition of her past seven years services as teacher. The Rev. T. W. Barber said he I had great pleasure in thanking Miss Taylor for her valuable services to the mission. He was sure she had fully realized the responsibility of her work in the preaching of the Gospel to the young ladies, and was also proud to say that she had accomplished her work 'as well if not better than her predecessors. He thanked Miss Thornton and all the members of the band for offering their services voluntarily to play for the dancing during the evening. Mr. Barber then presented the rose bowl to Miss Taylor amidst loud applause. Miss Taylor in reply, said that she was filled with gratitude for the words Mr. Barber had spoken and also expressed her thanks to the young ladies for their magnificent gift. She said it was a great pleasure to her to teach snob a class of well- behaved, kind, and friendly girls. -dg Woods' Great Peppermint Cure, for Cqughs and Colds; never fails. 1/1.1, 2/IL—Advt.

div.head: ST HELENS.
div.p: ST HELENS.
WORKS FIRE AT WARRINGTON.

Shortly after five o'clock on Wednesday night, infor- mation was received by telephone at the Fire Engine Station to the effect that a fire had broken out at the rope and twine works of Mr. Joseph Craik, Gray-street, off Hopwood-street. The fire bell WO9 rung and the whole of the men turned out very smartly, with a steam fire engine and ladders. On their arrival they found the works, which comprises a number of wooden buildings with tarred roofs, and are full of machinery and yarn, ablaze. The fireman quickly got to work from the closest hydrant but the supply of water was poor. Other hydrants were brought into use and a long line of hose was required to get the steamer working. Meanwhile numbers of willing helpers were removing the furniture from Mr. Craik's house and other cottages which adjoin the works. In spite of the great heat, the firemen stuck manfully to their won, and prevented the cottages from suffering any damage with the exception of broken windows and blistering of the paint on the doors and windows. The fire was checked before it spread to the tar-coated sheds off School Brow and Messrs. Rylands Bros.' netting shop. The emyloyees of the latter firm had their fire appiratus in readiness to render any assistance they could to the brigade, but their services were not required. The , Chief Constable, Superintendent Monaghan, and a large staff of police kept the great crowd of people from interfering with the task of the firemen. After two houra' work the fire was got under con- trol. The principal part of the works, with valuable machinery and a large quantity of yarn was gutted and the damage is estimated at several hundreds of pounds, which is covered by insurance. Mr. Craik was cut of town on business and was not aware of the disaster, the cause of which seems to be quite accidental, It is stated that one of the boys was lighting a gas, on which there was no burner, with a piece of tar-ropo. Startled by the blaze which flared up, the boy quickly withdrew his band and the lighted rope dropped on eozue yarn which immediately caught fire.

div.head: Workingmen's . Mission.
div.p: Workingmen's . Mission.

On Sunday afternoon a Epeeist service was held in this mission for the purpose of introducing the new hymn book (Garret Horder's Worship Song ') which has been adopted for use in the chapel. There was a large attendance. Alderman Bennett, who presided, said the new hymn book contained one of the finest selections he had ever seen. John Wesley, in his famous preface to the first edition of the Wesleyan hymn book, had pointed out that, there were two essentials for a book of that character. One was that it should be animated by the spirit of poetry arid the other that it should be animated by the spirit of piety. He (Alderman Bennett) thought he might fairly claim that the present hymnal satisfied both those conditions. There were many hymns which were extremely popular on account of the music with which they were associated but which were entirely unpoetic and very often little better than doggrel, and he was particularly glad to find that" Worship Song " not only included some of the best productions of the greatest hymnologists of all ages, but many of the finest poems of the leading poets of England and America. There were, be was pleased to notice, a large number of hymns by John Greenleaf Wiaittier,the grand old Quaker poet, the centenary of whose birth had recently been commemorated. In his opinion there was no hymn writer who gave truer expression to the genuine spirit •of religion,/ and more admirably exemplified the best spirit of true piety. The exact interpreta- tion of piety varied with the changing centuries and our present methods of giving expres- sion to it were somewhat different from those which were in vogue in Wesloy's time. But the funda- mental spirit was the same and he rejoiced to think that by the adoption of the new hymn book the con- gregation who worshipped in the mission would be so greatly helped in their desire to understand and to attain the essential spirit of Christianity.- Selections from the new book were sung by the choir which was uugumented by a juvenile choir, Mr. F. Atkinson pre- siding at the organ. Mr. T. Dale, on behalf of the workers, thanked Alderman Bennett for his kindness n attending. At the morning and evening services the preacher was Mr. T. Worthington, of Wigan.

div.head: CHAMBER OF COMMERCE. -- WARRINGTON BRIDGE QUESTION DISCUSSED.
div.p: CHAMBER OF COMMERCE. -- WARRINGTON BRIDGE QUESTION DISCUSSED.
Lively Passages.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce was held at the Town Hall on Thursday, Mr. G. Holman Kingdon (president) presiding. Taere were also present :—The Niztyor (Alderman Smethurst), Councillor Fulton-Smith, Messrs. C. E. Parker, L. Henshall, J. Jarman, ILT. Fairclough, C. U. Piarkinson, Segar Owen, H. Grosvenor, J. H. Smethurst, 0. Loft- house, J. Brandreth and Lewis, with Alderman Bennett (secretary).
ANNUAL REPORT. WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL.

• ----- - I The SECRETARY presented the thirty-first annual report of the Council which stated that they had made renewed efforts to induce the Ship Canal Company to facilitate the use of the lay-by at Stag Bridge, and to arrange that some of the principal coasting steamers should call at Warrington, believing that any develop- ment of local traffic would be equally in the interests of the town and the Canal Company. They were glad to report that a proper approach had been made to the lay-by and the electric light installed and that a suit- able warehouse had been provided. So long ago as April last the Council, who had previously com- municated with several leading shipping lines, requested the Ship Canal Company to assist them in definitely arranging for at least one line of steamers to regularly stop at Warrington as an experiment, but they were informed that thearr+nge- ments of the Company for dealing suitably with local cargoes without undue detention of the steamers, were not sufficiently advanced to enable them to comply with the suggestion, and the matter was still in abey- ance. They were greatly pleased to be able to record that the long and tedious litigation between the Canal Company and the local traders had ended in a complete victory for the latter. Henceforth they had secured to them for all time a navigable river channel with a minimutnidepth of Bft. at all stages of the tide. That highly controversial matter having been disposed of,the Council trusted that the Canal Company,the Corporation and the traders might work together in a spirit of mutual accommodation, and that no effort would be spared on either side to develop an increasing local traffic and to make Warrington an important shipping centre.

RAILWAY FACILITIES. In the month of July, the Council approached the Cheshire Lines Committee, in the hope of obtaining a better evening train service from Liverpool. The committee admitted the inconvenience of the existing arrangements, but stated that the probable financial results did not seem to justify the provision of the facilities the Chamber asked for.

BRIDGE QUESTIONS. The Council very much ree'retted-that the alterations at Bank Quay station which had long been promised were still delayed. They notice I that the Bridge at Wilderspool was to be widened and they considered that it would be a great advantage to the town if a new bridge at a high level could be erected, and the level crossing at kVilderspool abdlished, as it was a constant source of danger and inconvenience. The time seemed opportune as the Corporation had long been contem- plating the widening of Warrington Bridge,an improve- ment which was surely needed, and the two schemes might procee;.! together. A bridge across the river at Howley would also afford additional facilities for local trade.

div.head: M. LLOYD GEORGE AND THE RAILWAY DISPUTEI
div.p: M. LLOYD GEORGE AND THE RAILWAY DISPUTEI

It was unanimously resolved that a copy of the fol- lowing resolution be forwarded to the Right Hon. D. Lloyd George, M.P.: "That the Council of the Warrior,- ton Chamber of Commerce desire to place on record their high appreciation of the services rendered to the country gene ally, and to the commercial conununity in particular by the President of the Board of Trade in securing an equitable and far-sighted settlement of the recent railway dispute,—and hope that his action may be taken as a precedent in cases of similar industrial disputes in the future."

USEFUL LEGISLATION. The Secretary was continually receiving from the Board of Trade important information as to large cdn- tracts all over the world, and prompt particulars of these had been forwarded to any of the firms connected with the Chamber which were likely to be interested. Much valuable commercial literature was also continu- ally coming to hand, and might be seen at any time on application. The Council were glad to know that the Patents Act, the Mercantile Shipping Act, the Limited Partnership Act and other useful commercial measures which had long been advocated by the commercial community had been passed during the year, and that the imperial Government was increasingly recognising the importance and the utility of Chambers of Com- merce, alike in their collective and individual capacity. Inasmuch as the influence and importance of any Chamber must depend upon the extent to which it was supported by he town to which it belonged, the Council were glad to be able to announce that the membership again showed an increase, and that the financial position was satisfactory.
.FINANCIAL. The balance sheet showed that an adverse balance of £2 15s. lid. had been converted into a credit balance of .£2 10s. od. . . . .
The report and balance sheet were adopted on the proposition of the CITAIRNI IN. seconded by Mr. LOFIAOUSE.
WARRINGTON BRIDGE. LIVELY DISCUSSION.

Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGH introduced the question of Warrington Bridge. He said everybody was of opinion that an improvement was necessary for the conveni- ence of pedestrian and vehicular traffic. He would, however, emphasise the importance of the question frmn the commercial standpoint. The utilisation of the waterway was of value to the town not only on account of the volume of river traffic but because it had the effect of keeping the railway rates down. Then with regard to sea-borne traffic via Liverpool, cargoes for Warrington were sent to Manchester where certain dues were charged and then the goods were brought back to Warrington free. There had lately been a great deal of litigation about the dredging of the river and the result was that an Bft. channel had to be maintained. The traders, however, were not getting the full benefit of it because Warrington Bridge was so constructed that only small craft could pass under it. The bridge was therefore an incubus on trade and the sooner it was altered the better it would be for manufacturers. There was a prevalent idea that it would only effect Messrs. Fairclongh and Sons but he had shown how it would effect all the traders in War- rington. He moved a resolution to the effect that it was desirable that a new bridge should be substituted for the present structure. Mr. SEGAR OwENT : Will Mr. Fairclough include in his resolution that it shall be a one span bridge,because that is the great point as far as he is concerned. Mr. PAIRCLOUGIf : I don't mind whether it is two spans or one so long as we are able to navigate under- neath it. Mr. PARKINSON asked how the railway bridge affected the traffic ? Mr. Fatuc,Lonoti : It does not affect it at all. Mr. PARKINSON said he had seen boats stopped at the bridge, brit Mr. Fairclough said they were waiting for tidal changes. Mr. JARMAN said there would not be much gained by spending a big sum on a new bridge if the railway bridge then stood in the way. Alderman BENNETT : There is always the possibility of an ultimate improvement of the railway bridge. Mr. LoFrHousE seconded Mr. Fairclough's proposi- tion. He said that what appealed to them and certainly to the man in the street more than river transit was

the crowded, dangerous state of traffic over the bridge. When he first came to Warrington it seemed to him to be a scandal that a town of such importance, doing such a large business,and which mis an ambitious town, should be bottled up in the shocking ignominious way in which all traffic was blocked at Wlrrington bridge. Councillor FULTON SmtTH said the railway rates were a very strong point to manufacturers. It was through the Ship Canal being so near Warrington that they had been able to check the very high rates. If they could
PRESIDENTIAL ADDRESS.
THE QUESTION OF INFANTILE MORTALITY.

In his Presidential address Mr. KINGDON dealt specially with his work as the representative of the Chamber on the Education Committee. He said : The object of education is neither the passing of examina- tions nor the making of money, but from the point of view of one who would like to hear the doctrine of the dignity of labour preiched more often, rather the attainment of that happiness which is the product of a well-ordered mind amidst reasonably comfortable surroundings, although we must not forget that in towns like ours, consisting largely of an industrial population, the principal inducement to the young to take advantage of the educational facilities that are olerad to them will be the chance of an improvement in their position in life, with all its attendant advan- tages. The rising generation of to-day will be the rank and file, and in some cases no doubt the captains as well, of our industrial army of to-morrow. How necessary, then, that we should satisfy ourselves that the younger portion of the staffs that we employ are being equipped with the educational weapons that will enable them to acquit themselves creditably in the industrial warfare in which they will have, to take part later on and which bids fair to become at least no less keen as the years pass by. I wish here to say IL word on a subject which is very dear tome,

INFANT MORTALITY, or rather the prevention of it. Our commercial men are anxious enough in their own businesses to prevent waste in any form; why do they not concern themselves with the worst of all waste, National waste ? Our record in Warrington in this respect is nothing to boast about. With a high Infant Mortality little or nothing has been done in the way of preventive measures, although other towns, and notably Huddersfield, have set themselves to tackle the problem in earnest. There through the spirit of one of their public men combined with the untiring assistance of their Medical Officer of Health and a band of willing lady helpers, results have been produced which to-day make their town famous in this connection. The scheme according to particulars for which I am indebted to scheme, Alderman Broadbent, M.A., .1.1'., rests mainly on giving to each mother a Promissory Note for £l,payable on proof that the child is fit and healthy on attaining the age of twelve months. Years ago Rudderstield went to Parliament to acquire ' power for the Compulsory Notification of Births within 12 hours, without which the scheme would have been impossible, while Wan ington to-day is still undecided whether to adopt what is now in many other places the law of the land. div.p: ED LTC AT EONAL WASTE

........ and I must pass on. The school life ends at 11, in some cases even earlier. It is often the case that the child then gets no more attention or mental training at all ; he becomes a wage-earner and is left to shift for him- self. Again I ask you what wotild be thought of the man who planted and cherished a seedling into vigorous growth and then stopped watering it when just due to flower? And-yet this is precisely what we are ding all Over the country. Many a lad for the sake of the temporary benefit of bringing a few shillings extra to the home has been permanently disadvantagvd. Is this not a matter where our commercial men can be of real assistance ? Why should not every employer consider himself responsible for the continued education of the lads in his service ? Compulsion is not only legitimate but desirable when National interests are at stake. I plead here as I have done in other places for every erayloyer to make attendance at Evening Schools up to 17 or 18, in co-operation with the local Director of Education, a condition of employment. Passing on to commercial matters, Mr. KINGDON said :—ln other directions we have : The Limited Partnership Act and the Company Law Amendment Act, both of which are deserving of the closest attention. The Lights on Vehicles Act, makes it compulsory that every moving vehicle after dark shall show light. The Trades Disputes Bill and the new Workmen's Com- pensation Act bring to mind the difficulties during the past year in the railway world, the loss to our trade and the dislocation to business generally such as would have resulted from the TFIREATENED RAILWAY STRIKE

.. happily averted by the intervention of the Board of Trade. I view that settlement with perfect satisfac- tion, first because it shows the time is past when the Presidency of that Department can be held by gentle- men who on account of services to their party, either real or imaginary, or because of influence or agreeable social qualities, were considered to be entitled to one of the lesser plums from the Ministerial tree—a state of affairs with which it is almost incredible we should have put up so long ; for even if we are called on the Continent 'The Nation of Shopkeepers' why at least should we not have the satisfaction of running our nation like a successful business, and what is a nation but a business on a large scale? And secondly because just as labour is necessary to capital, so is capital to labour. The two together make an integral whole, but

div.head: PRESENTATION TO MR. AND MRS. A. H CROSFIELD
div.p: PRESENTATION TO MR. AND MRS. A. H CROSFIELD
To Take Place Next Wednesday.

The presentation to the Borough Member and his wife, subscribed to by all sections of the Liberal Party in Warrington, will be made at a great Liberal demonstration in Parr Hall next Wednesday. The present will take the form of an illuminated address, and a handsome, upright grand Steinway piano. Both the Member and his wife are accomplished musicians, and the gift should be very appropriate. Mr. C. E. Parker will preside and. Mrs. Parker will make the presentation. Speeches will be delivered by Mr. C. E. Parker (on behalf of the Liberal Association), Mrs. Parker (on behalf of the Women's Association), Alder- man Tinnion (on behalf of the Liberal Club), and Mr. Joseph Elwell (on behalf of the Progressive Labour League.) A grand concert will follow, the artistes being Miss Alice Woodland (soprano), Miss Lily Fairhurst (contralto), Mr. Harris (bass), Mr. J. Rabbitt (tenor), the Lyric Prize Quartet, and the Co-operative Glee Party. Mr. J. Forster will be the accompanist.

div.head: DINNER TO WORKPEOPLE.
div.p: DINNER TO WORKPEOPLE.

On Friday evening Mr. and Crosfield will entertain the employees of Messrs. Joseph Crostield and Sons, Ltd., at dinner. Six hundred will sit down at the Parr Mil, and another GOO will be catered for in the works dining hall. Whilst the meal is in progress the brass band will play selections at the Purr Hall and the orrliestra will provide music at the works. At eight o'clock the whole of the employees will assemble in the Parr Hall and there will be a musical enter- tainment and some speech-making.

div.head: Services for Sunday.
div.p: Services for Sunday.

I Holy rrinity Church: Morning 10.30, the Bishop of the Diocese will preach, whilst in the evening the pulpit will be occupied by the Rev. Horace Gray, M.A„ head- master of the Grammar School. In the afternoon at 2.45 a service for scholars will be held. The collections throughout the day will be to defray the expenses of repairing the fabric of the church on the south side and rebuilding the vestry. £6O is required for the work. Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay: Preacher, morn- ing 11.0, evening 6.0, Mr. J. Jamieson, secretary, Temperance Legislation League, Manchester District. Wycliffe Church, Bewsey-street : Morning 10.30, evening 6.30, Rev. J. Yonge. Bold-street Wesleyan Church : Morning 10.30, Rev. Sidney Pitt ; evening 6.30, Rev. Thomas Miller. Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church : Home Missions. Preacher, morning 10 30 and evening 6.30, Rev. Richard W. Allen (secretary of the Army and Navy Board). Golborne-street Baptist Church : Morning 10.45 and evening 6.30, Rev. E. G. Gauge, F.R.A.S., of London. En the afternoon at 2.30 a United Service will be held when the chair will be taken by Mr. J. Jarman and an address will be given by the Rev. J. F. Matthews. Baptist Church. Latchford : Morning 10.30 and evening 6.0, Rev. J. F. Matthews.

div.head: FORTHCOMING LICENSING
div.p: THE FORTHCOMING LICENSING
BILL.
Resolution by Liberal Women.

The Warrington Women's Liberal Association have this wpek passed a resolution in view of the Licensing Bill to he early introduced by the Government and sent copies to the Premier, Mr. Asquith, and Mr. A. H. Crostleld The resolution is as follows.

_ . " That this meeting of the Warrington Women's Liberal Association bath with satisf4ction the declara- tion that it is the intention of the Government to reverse the retrograde Licensing Act passed by the Conservatives in 1904 by bringing in a comprehensive measure of Temperance reform as the first measure of the Session; and expresses its strong conviction that if the Bill is to be acceptable to the great body of reformers in the country, it must include provisions for National Sunday Closing, for excluding children from public-houses, and for conferring upon the people in every locality throughout Great Britain the power to prevent by their direct votes the issue and renewal of licLuor licences."

div.head: WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVES.
div.p: WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVES.
Candidate Adopted.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Conservative Association was held on Thursday night in the Assembly room of the Conservative Club, Sankey-street, Sir Gilbert Greenall,Art., presiding over a good attend- ance. . . . .

In the annual report submitted by the hon. secretary (Mr. E. J. Hall), allusion was made to the reorganisation of the party, which was now nearly com- plete. New committees had been appointed in every ward, under the leadership af chairmen, vice-chairmen, and honorary secretaries of influence,loyalty and energy. The result of the re-organisation had, so far tested,been highly satisfactory. Reference was also made to the successes which the Conservative party had achieved in municipal elections since the last meeting, and it was a record of which the party might well be proud. (Applans..) The report of the HON. TREASURER ( Mr. Segar Owen) was also read, being of a satisfactory character. Sir Gilbert Greenall was unanimously re-elected president. Mr. W. P. R.ylands was elected chairman, Mr. E. J. Hall secretary. and Mr. Segar Owen treasurer. Mr. W. P. Rylands proposed that Mr. Robert Pier- point, ex-M.P. for the borough of Warriugton, be adopted as the prospective candidate for the Conser- vative party at the next election. He remarked that Mr. Pierpoint had served the party faithfully and well for 14 years until the election in 190(1. Mr. Pierpoint I was a follower of Mr. Balfour as regarded fiscal policy. The resoultion was seconded by Councilior FULEON Smrrn, and carried with enthusiasm.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.-
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.-
"Dick Whittington."

There will be an exceptionally fine attraction at the Palace and Hippodrome next week when 111 r. John Tiller's Christmas pantomitne "Dick Whittington and his Cat " will be presented. The show will be on a lavish scale, with specially painted scenery and beauti- ful dresses The cJaipany is a strong one, including Rene Howard as princip tl boy. There will be seven scenes and the pantomime promises to be one of the brightest and prettiest ever seen in Warrington. Matinees are announced for Thursday anti Saturday at 2.30. The evening performances commence at 7 I and 9 o'clock.

GUILD CONCERT.—On Thnrsday evening a grand concert was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom under the auspices of the Wesley Guild. Mr. Jenks occupied the chair, and hi his remarks said how grateful the members of the Guild were to Mr. and Mrs. Stevenson who had been the means of providing several of the artistes, who came from Lancaster. div.head: LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY.
div.p: LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY.
Clerical Staff Dinner.
THE LABOUR PARTY AND SOCIALIST

Sir, —The passing of the Socialist resolution by the Labour Party has aroused uneasiness and displeasure in many a tranquil bosom. It has evoked criticism and advice in generous quantities. In all probability there will be a split, so we are told. I notice already there is talk about secession and refusals to associate with the resolution but I am also conscious the trouble is magnified. But I know through contact with trade unionists there is likely to be dissension, hence this effusion. I iinagine, the individual who is wrathful he threatens to withdraw his support, he has no desire to have connection whatever with such a detestable doctrine as Socialism and if you ask him what books he has real dealing with Socialism, he would no doubt find it awkward to state. Perhaps the obsolete method of strike suits him as yet. His position is lamentable. The tide unionist who cannot see the futility of the strike must have faith illimitable. When we weigh together the cost, the anxiety, starvation, and the return Obtained when successful, we wonder is it worth it? The development in industrial organisation, the decentralisation of capital is rendering it impera- tive that some better method should be devised, and Labour representation presents itself as a most feasible plan. To prove the superiority of the two methods one illustration will suffice. Compare the cost of strike and litigation in connection with the Taff Vale dispute, which was unsuccessful, and the cost of returning thirty odd Labour Members whose efforts were successful. Well, suppose now our friend is convinced af the necessity of a Labour Party and we have a sufficiently strong party elected to dominate business of Parliament. They have passed into law what the average trade unionist agrees with —old-age pensions, graduated income tax, taxation of land values, &c. Does our friend believe/hat to be the end of the usefulness of a Labour Party? If not in what direction will it move ? The resolutions adopted by trade unions themselves supply the answer. The railway servants favour railway ,nationalising, the miners want mine nationalisation, and most of the Labour M.P.'s who repudiate Socialism subscribe their adherence to land nationalisation. Sir John Brunner has stated that private enterprise in canals is a failure and I suppose Sir John can be considered a mouth- piece for the capitalist class. And one wonders what will be left of the Socialist's programme of the "public ownership of the means of production, distribution and exchange " when, these estimable gentlemen have finished. Another question which presents itself to me is: why do these people reject a principle under one name, and accept it under another? The situation is amazing.
LABOR OHNIA VINCIT. A FREE-BOOTING EXPEDITION.

A large part of the misery of our civilized life arises out of the squalid insufficiencies of which the misery of bad blots is perhaps the simplest example. A lot of people are prepared to say that such miseries cannot be avoided. They will say that every one cannot have the best of things' that of all sorts of good things, including good leather and cobbling there is not enough to go round, that lower class people ought not to mind being shabby and uncom- fortable, in fact that they ought to be very glad to be able tO live at all

Such arguments are not to be swept aside with a wave of the hand. Everyone cannot have the best of things; it is in the nature of things that some boots should be better and some worse. Nobody dreams of a time when everybody will have exactly as good boots as everyone else, and .any such childish equality is impossible. It is one thing. however, to recognise that there must be a certain picturesqueness and variety in foot wear. It is quite another thing to admit that a large majority of people can never hope to be more thin uncomfortably shod in painful unhealthy and unsightly shoddy. The last proposi- , tion is inadmissible. There is enough good leather in the world to make good sightly boots, enough men at leisure and enough power and machinery to do all the work required, enough unetuployed intelligence to organise the shoemaking and shoe distribution for everyone. _

What stands in the way ? On the one hand, in any unfashionable part of Great Britain and elsewhere, are numbers of people needing boots ; on the other are great stretches of land of huge possibilities of cattle and leather, and great numbers of people, who either through riches or trade disorder, are doing no work. The question is, "Why cannot the people be set to work and make and distribute boots ?" Come with me on an imaginary Free Booting Expedition. Wego to South America to get leather and begin at the beginning by setting to work to kill and flay a herd of cattle. You are at once interrupted. Your first obstacle is a man who says the cattle and leather belong to him. We explain the leather is wanted in England for people who have no decent boots. He does not care a rap what we want it for, and says so with crimson trimmings. We have to buy him off. It is his private property, this leather and lands and catt e. If you ask him how much he wants for his leather he frankly tells you " As much as your need will compel you to give." We say to him, 'But how did you come by these herds, this land, so that you can stand between the people and them and exact this profit ? " Being a rude and violent person he would probably lose his temper and decline to answer, and while admitting lie deserves a reasonable fee Lr the care he had taken of the land and herds, we find such an admission does not satisfy him. It is not a reasonable reward, for service rendered, that he wants. He wants his profit and we buy him off eventually and proceed to get the leather here, to England. We bring it by rail and ship, and thereby again come in contact with people who have no desire of helping our project, who stand in our course, resolved to make every possible penny out of us in our attempt to provide sound boots for everyone. The railway was private property and had an owner pr owners— the same with the ship. Such owners are not satisfied with a mere fee adequate to their services. They also are determined to make every penny profit out of you and me. The real owners are probably quiescent shareholders whose functiou appears to he to recline and to possess. Well, Well ! We get the leather to England and proceed to a centre of population, invite workers to erect sheds and machinery upon a vacant piece of ground ; and in a state of generous industry start in to provide boots. Ali ! but do we An owner comes along and demands an enormous price for the land. The workers cannot get house room until they pay rent—every inch of the blessed earth seems to be someb .dy's property and we pay: pay, pay. One might run on indefinitely in this strain. There could be plenty of leather, and there certainly is- plenty of labour and intelligence in the world to manage boots and many other clesirabl% things. But this institution of private 'property in land and naturally produced things,these obstructive claims that prevent us using the ground, or moving material, and that have to be bought out, stand in the way. We seek a remedy and though lies abound yet truth is said to lie at the bottom of WELLS.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

VISIT OF THE REV. J. E. RATTENnunv.—On Tuesday evening in connection with the Wesley Guild, a lecture was given in the Wesleyan Church, Padgate, by the Rev. J. E. Rattenbury of the Loudon Missions on "The Church and the People." The chapel was tilled by a very large congregation, many having come from War- rington and the surrounding districts. The rev.gentleman during the course of his lecture demonstrated his case from historical review that the great reforming move- ments of modern ages had arisen when the gospel had been preached to the poor —as Christ's mission had been particularly directed to them, although it had at the same time embraced all humanity. Nlr.Rattenbury made a powerful appeal to his hearers to see that they had practical sympathy with the poorer brothers and sisters by assisting in removing the social evils in their midst and also not to hesitate forming association with them, and thus follow the example of their great Leader Jesus Christ who was always the friend of the social outcast of His times. Mr. Meldrum of Lymm, occupied the chair and Mr. Alderman Bennett, the Rev. T. Miller and Rev. W. Mellor also took part in the meeting.

div.p: Warrington did not win quite as easily as expected, but they had much more of the game than a score of 5 points to 2 would indicate. Chances were missed which should have been turned to good account, but the game was a good one to wa;:rh for all that. The first half saw Warrington attacking almost contin-, uously with a strong wind behind them. Fish made three good runs but failed to get • over the line, and Isherwood's try came very suddenly. Brooks took a pass from Lloyd and Isherwood dashed up at right angles to the half- back. He received the ball when on the run and swerving in the opposite direction to Brooks he bluffed the Broughton centres finely and went through near the posts with as good a try as any he has recorded in his long career. Fish carefully kicked a goal and this was all the scoring up to the interval.

I The Rangers, who had played a smart game seemed to have a bright prospeot on changing ends. For a few minutes they were all over Warrington, and Claude James had an open field once but hesitated when he should have trusted to his speed to beat Tilley. Then Warrington woke up and played in surprising style against the wind. Even the Rangers' long , kicking did not avail them, for the home lot showed ' great staying power and drove the opposition back every time. Brooks made the run of the game but spoiled the effort by failing to pass. Had he been speedier lie was certain to score, but for a solo effort half the length of the field, Brooks needs to be about two seconds faster in the "100." Isherwood was not quite so good in this half, and missed one or two good passes, Broughton found the home three- quarter line altogether too solid to get past, and a penalty wial by Harris was their only reward for much exertion.

An auspicious oommencement under the Northern Union was made by F. G. Jenkins, the Newport forward, who wore the Warrington colours for the first time. Tb: • well-built young player showed unmistakable evidenc 38 of class, and was ever to the fore with the Warrington van guard. Lloyd shaped well at the 1: .se of the scrum, but was weak in tackling. On the right wing Taylor seemed out of place. Flynn was the best of the Broughton backs, 'though praise is due to the young full back, Hall, who filled Barlow's place with such credit. On the right wing Flardynian showed speed, but found Fish rather more than he could manage. The Warrington crack is still very heavy, but he can run and swerve a bit yet !

Oldham still remain unbeaten at the head of the league. How I wish they had to come to Warrington again ! Hunslet were beaten at Salford on Saturday, and at Merthyr on Monday, but they still remain a good second. Wigan's recent misfortunes have not yet told heavily on their percentage, while Broughton, Keighley and Salford all lead Warrington. The Wilderspool men have, however, an excellent chance of climbing over the next three I should like to see them contesting the League championship. They would not be without backers—though the prospect on Oldham territory would scarcely be dazzling.

TO-DAY'S MATCH. Warrington visit Leeds to-day, to play the first of three successive away matches, and they ought to win. Leeds are not the team they were a year ago, and most of the hacks are comparatively inexperienced players It should be recalled by the Warrington team that they were beaten last season at Headingley by no less than 27 points to 3. They therefore owe Leeds a drubbing, and the team selected should be capable of doing the needful

The team is :—Tilley, full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson and Watkins, three-quarters ; Taylor and Brooks, half-backs ; Thomas, Boardman, P. Board- man, Jenkins, Heath and Belton, forwards. This is almost a powerful as team as Warrington can put in the field, with the exception of Shugars for Belton. The big Welshman has not, however, got his damaged leg in order yet. I am glad Taylor has been moved to half-back; the position should suit him much better than wing, for he is essentially an inside player. On the rfght, Watkin gets his chance in senior company, and I hope he will have a little luck— that gees such a long way to the making of a player. Jenkins, the half-back, is likely to be another three or four weeks before he is sound again. The injury to his knee is rather serious.

There is nothing Inure sensational at Wilderspool to-day than a friendly with Egerton, who were beaten a fortnight ago by 413 points. Warrington are trying a local lad named Craddock on the wing, and the team is : —Jordan, full back ; Tinkler, Kenyon, Cartwright and Craddock, three-quarters ; Lloyd and Daintith, half-backs; Jolley, Foster, Holbrook, Fair- hurst, Kettle, and Bradshaw forwards.

div.p: MATCH ON MCNDAY.

....... On Monday, Salford pay their postponed visit to Warrington. The match should arouse keen interest, as Salford are next above Warrington in the League table. The kick-off will be at 3 o'clock, rather r.n early hour for a mid-week gams. -- VIE SECOND IEsT. The second of the series of three test matches between the All Blacks and the Northern Union will be played at Chelsea on February 8, and on Tuesday the following team was chosen to represent the Union : Back-.—H. Taylor (Hull). hree-quarter backs. —P. Eccles (Halifax), T. Llewellyn (Oldham), B. Jenkins (Wigan), J. Leytham (Wigan). Half-backs.—J. Jolley (Runcorn) and J. Baxter (Rochdale Hornets). Forwards. —A.Smith (Oldham),H. Wilson (Flunslet), G. Ruddick (Broughton Rangers), D. Jones (Merthyr), S. Warwick (Salford), and G. Thomas (Warrington). Reserves : G. Dickenson (Warrington), and J. Spencer (Salford).

At last Warrington have a representative in one of the test teams. After going to Leeds as reserve last Saturday, Thomas deserved a place. Apart from this, however, there is no better forward in the Northern Union than this year's N.U. Welsh captain. G. Dickenson will also accompany the party to London as reserve threequarter. I hope to see him picked for the third test at Cheltenham.

So far the All Blacks have only won one of their fixtures against renresentative teams the one against Yorkshire. On Saturday they were defeated for the 13th time, the first test match at Leeds proving rather too much for them. Just now, the All Blacks are feeling the effects of the heavy pro- gramme they have gone through, and it would have been better to have played some of the big games earlier.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

BAND OF HOPE ENTERTAINMENT.—On Monday evening the fourth entertainment of the season in connection with the Hill Cliffe and Stockton Heath United Band of Hope was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. The Rev. J. S. Hughes presided over a good attendance, and was supported on the platform by Mr. Arthur Mounfleld (one of the vice-presidents of the society), and Mr. G. Whitfield (secretary). Mr. Mounfleld gave an address, in which he spoke of the early associations of the movement with Stockton Heath. After pointing out the dangers of moderation he appealed to all present to come over to to the side of total abstinence. A Rood programme was submitted, rc3itations being credit ably given by E. Bennett, NV. Powell, M. Forsyth J. Williams, 0. tliffe, G. Nicholls, T. Gamble, L. Powell, E. Julian and E. Ham blett, the latter reciting very feelingly "Billy's rose," whilst Miss M. Whitmore gave a capital rendering of "The last hymn." Songs were well given by M. Monnfield, Edith Hamblett, and A. Cliffe. An action song, entitled "Little Nurses " by E. Whitfield, D. Maile, L. Pollitt, A. Forsyth, D. Cain, and Rathbone (who had been trained by two of the elder girls) was much enjoyed. A dialogue entitled "Bridget's Errand " was well given by A. Mounfleld, G. Hamblett, M. Isherwooe, A. Hughes and A. Whitfield. The event of the evening was the humorous temperance dialogue, "Paddy's Pledge" which provoked roars of laughter.and the characters were taken by the Misses L. Hall, I. Ellison, E. Whitfield, G. Gould and W. Wilkes. Mr. G. A. Whitfield acted as accompanist.

div.head: HEREDITARY PAUPERISM.
div.p: HEREDITARY PAUPERISM.

It was reported to the Forden (Mongotneryshire) Board of Guardians on Wednesday, that one pauper had been in the Workhouse since 1840, and another pauper had been receiving out-relief since 1805. No less than dye-sixths of the permanent paupers in one district were hereditary paupers, paupers because their parents were.

div.head: VERDICT.
div.p: THE VERDICT.

The following was the verdict returned by a Bolton jury on Wednesday at the inquest on a man named John Peers : Death due to hesrt failure as a result of chronic bronchitis, accelerated by a wound in his throat, self- inflicted with a knife whilst,in a state of delirium as a result of his illness.

MY DEAR CHILDREN, I am very pleased to be able to announce the winners in the Poor Children's Competition. It has been so successful, and the clothing so acceptable to many poor little children, that the competition will be continued during January and February, and prizes will be awarded for the best articles received. JERUSALEM. Fallen is thy throne, 0 Israel: Silence is o'er thy plains; Thy dwellings all lie desolate; Thy children weep in chains. Where are the clews that fed thee? On Etham's barren shore? That fire from Heaven which led thee Now lights thy path no more. Lord, Thou didst hive Jerusalem! The wild wind whirls away. Silent and waste her bowers

div.head: CAN'T STOP.
div.p: CAN'T STOP.

- - An English canon of note used to tell a good story of himself, in his Capacity of r.•:agistrate he was once visiting the county gaol, and ex- Patiated to a friend who was with him on the virtues of the treadmill. Warming with his theme, he declared that he often wished he had one at home to give him the gentle exercise he required, hut WII4 too lazy to take, except under compulsion; and, to remove his friend's scepti- cism, he asked t he warder to give him a turn. Round went the mill, the canon declaring that the movement was delightful; but after two minutes of it he had had quite enough, and called on the officer to stop the mill. To his horror the officer ahswered:— " Very sorry, sir; I can't. It's timed to go fifteen minutes, and won't stop before."

Frederick William, father of Frederick the Great, of Prussia, painted, or fancied he painted, but his works were mere daubs. Such, however, was not the language of his courtiers. when descanting on the merits, of the royal Apelles. On one occasion his Majesty favoured them with the sight of a new specimen. "Sup- pose," said the King, "that some great painter —Rubens or Raphael, for instance—had painted this picture, do you think it would fetch a con- siderable price?" "Sire," replied the Baron de Polnitz, who passed for the most practised. and most obsequious of his Majesty's courtiers, "I assure you that a connoisseur could not offer Less for such a picture than twenty-five ,housand florins." " Well, then, Baron," cried. , .ttified monarch, "you shall receive a ' my munificence. Take the picture for sand florins, which you shall pay me in, ..)ney ; and, as I wish to render you a 2er-

„u have my permission to sell it again.” An, sire," returned the Baron, who was fairly caught in his own snare, "I can never consent to take advantage of your Majesty's generosity."' "No reply," said the King; " I know that I make you a handsome present, by which you will gain fifteen thousand florins or more. But. your zeal for my interest has been proved, and I owe you some recompense. Your love for the arts and your attachment to myself entitle ycu. to a mark of my esteem."

div.head: FUNNY STORY.
div.p: A FUNNY STORY.

Once upon a time a lady had two children ill with the measles. She knew a lady who could tcil her how to cure them, so she wrote and Asked her. There was another lady who wanted to know how to pickle onione. The woman re- ceived the letters safely, but she got them mixed. and sent the wrong ones out. The lady who wanted to know how to cure her children read as follows:—" Boil them three times in vinegar, sprinkle them with salt, and in a few ^.ys they will be ready."
DOROTHY CARMELL.
A farmer with children sixteen, Killed the fattest young lamb of his flock. To divide it these children between, What must be the time by the clock? Answer: A quarter to four. GEORGE COLWILL.

div.head: SARAH JANE.
div.p: SARAH JANE.

I'm feeling so sad and wretched, I think I could cry for a week. It's no use your saying, " Don't bother," I'll bear it no longer, I'll speak. I know very well I'm not pretty, Well, p'raps you might even say plain; And of course my name's not Phyllis Gertrude, But just plain, short Sarah Jane. Still, tell iie, pray, 'cause her hair's curly, And her cheeks are so pink and so white, Is it fair you should leave me neglected, And take her to bed of a night? Sc' long, oh, so long, I have loved you, I'm wooden, I know, but I'm true; A Lutch doll can love like a wax one,
Oh, mistress, I wish that you knew. Your poor Small Jane's broken-hearted, Do please take her back to her place; I love you far better than she Though she has got a prettier face. L. MAWER.

"•Sure, wasn't I to see what time the train started? And how was I to come back before she went?"

M. Kuckuck, of Leipsic, seems to have found the solution of the difficult problem of spontaneous generation quite easy. He has no great difficulty in making living crea- tures. And he has published, under the title of "Die Losung des Problems der Urzeu- gung," an account of his work. A mixture of gelatine, pepton, asparagin, glycerin, and sea-water is sterilised by boiling. Then a little barium chloride is added. This pro- duces ionisation, and ionisation leads to or- ganisation. At any rate, Kuckuck claims to have produced in this way minute bodies which feed, and grow, and forni cell-colonies. By adding barium chloride to fresh albumen, and also to yolk of egg, similar bodies were obtained. Kuckuck applies the result of his experiments to the solution of the question, What were the first organisms? He concludes that these were, non-nucleated Monera which appeared spontaneously in the sea through the ionisation brought about by a mixture of organic and inorganic substances. The weak point in the explanation, comments the Globe, is that before there were organisms there could not be organic substances. Until these experiments have been repeated by other ob- servers with like results they will probably not be received by biologists.

div.head: AVERAGES OF RAINFALL.
div.p: AVERAGES OF RAINFALL.

It is often very important to have some knowledge of the average rainfall of a place or district, for we are dependent upon the rainfall for our water supply. If observa- tions have only been made for a few years, the results w.,,t probably be wide of the true average, for rainfall being so very variable, the rainfall during the period over which the observations have been made may be con- siderably above or below the average, and so give too high or too low a mean. Dr. H. It. Mill, the Director of the British Rainfall Or- ganisation, has stated that at least thirty years' observations of rainfall are necessary for obtaining a true average.

div.head: NEARLY DEAD UNIVERSE.
div.p: A NEARLY DEAD UNIVERSE.

Mathematicians have tried their hands, as a recreation, at weighing all the stars, that is to say, finding the quantity of matter they all contain. They discovered a great fact— the mass of all visible stars in the greatest telescope is so small in comparison with the quantity of matter that mathematicians can feel, not see, that it may be almost neg- lected. Therefore, the main quantity of matter does not emit light. The universe is nearly dead. Photographs of the entire celes- tial vault reveal about 100,000,000 suns. These may be ignored. It is known to mathe- maticians that there is matter enough in existence to make 32,000,000,030 suns equally as massive as our own. Proof is had from velocities of rapid suns. This quantity of matter exists. A minute fraction appears in the form of visible suns. But what of the rest? Is it in dead suns, planets, and moons?

div.head: SPONTANEOUS GENERATION.
div.p: SPONTANEOUS GENERATION.
MARS AND ITS CANALS.
Leaving aside the older and now generally discredited explanations that the canals •are gigantic water-channels, that they are cracks in a universal covering of ice, and that they
are grooves- cut by colliding asteroids, and dealing with explanations held es snore pro- bablb by the astronomers of the present day, Professor W. H. Pickering, in Harper'

- Magazine, declares that much the oldest of these considers them to be caused by narrow ditches, which, crossing the desert regions of the planet, furnish water to vegetation grow- ing along their banks: It is these comparatively broad bands of vegetation, and not the narrow water-chan- nels themselves, which are visible in our tele- scopes. The chief advocate of this view at the present time is Professor Lowell, who has adopted it as the foundation of his theories of Martian civilisation. A serious OBJECTION TO THIS HYPOTHESIS

is the difficulty of forcing the water through the canals for thousands of miles over a com- paratively level country. Professor Lowell gets over this difficulty by stating that it is pumped through them artificially. Many astronomers recoil from an artificial explana- tion where it is possible to account for the phenomena observed by any natural method. The difficulty of transporting the water is further enhanced if we consider the fact, which is generally admitted, that the amount of atmosphere we find on Mars does not ex- ceed one-quarter the quantity per square mile of surface that we find upon the earth. This view is based largely on Professor Campbell's spectroscopic investigations, con- firmed by the clearness with which ire see the details of the planet's surface. Since gravity upon Mars is but three-eighths of what it is upon the earth, the

div.head: ATMOSPHERE PRESSURE
div.p: ATMOSPHERE PRESSURE

on the Martian surface cannot exceed three thirty-seconds of our own, or seventy-one millimetres of mercury. Under this low pressure water boils at 113 deg. Fahr. If the amount of atmosphere on Mars is only one- tenth as much as that on the earth, which is highly probable, the boiling-point of water upon the surface of the planet would be re- duced to 84deg. Fahr. That the daylight temperature of the surface does not differ greatly from our own we know by the rapidity with which the Polar ice-caps disap- pear on the approach of summer. It would, therefore, seem that the evaporation of water from the surface must proceed with etra,- ordinary rapidity, and the difficulty of trans- porting it through canals, and supplying sufficient for the needs of vegetation upon the way, must be accordingly greatly enhanced. Indeed, it would seem necessary to substi- , tote

div.head: GIGANTIC WATER-MAINS
div.p: GIGANTIC WATER-MAINS

for the canals, with a most extended system of supplementary piping. The amount of power required to pumii, sufficient water to irrigate anywhere berkeen 100,000 and 1,000,000 square miles of surface, through such a system of piping, may be left to any competent hydraulic engineer to compute, with the added statement that most, of the water is to be transported to a distance ex- ceeding 1,000 miles. The physical conditions on Mars are in many ways intermediate between those found upon the earth and the moon, and it seems plausible that the life existing upon it should similarly be of a higher type than that found on the moon, and of a lower type than that found at present on the surface of the earth. Even if the physical conditions, as we under- stand them, were equally favourable with times. on the earth, civilisation would by no means be a necessary consequence. Had it I not been settled by Europeans, tile United States would still be a wilderness. How much tess snoutd we hasten to accord civilisation to a planet of which we know little, except that if we were transported there ourselves, we should instantly die,

Saturday saw the first benefit match evcr given by the Warrington Football Club, the proceeds being set apart for Dan Isherwood, the popular left centre three- quarter who has worn the Warrington colours for over 12 years. Beautiful weather prevailed and there was a capital crowd of nearly 7,000, the receipts, including tickets totalling over £l9O. Broughton Rangers were the visitors, but neither team was quite at full strength. Warrington were without Jenkins, Thomas and Stingers, but gave a trial to F. G. Jenkins, a forward from Newport. Broughton's prin- cipal absentees were Hogg and Ruddick. The teams lined out as follows : Warrington—J. Tilley, back ;J. Fish, D. Isherwood (capt.), G. Dickenson and I. Taylor, three-quarter backs; E. Brooks and J. Lloyd, half backs ; P. Boardman, A. E. Boardman, G. Heath, F. G. Jenkins, W. Harmer, and W. Belton forwards. Broughton Rangers—H. Hall, back; W. Hardyman,; Barlow, C. James and Harris, three quarter backs / S. James and J. Flynn, half backs; J. Beetham, Darlison, Orem, Clompitt, Winskill and Mottram forwards. Referee, Mr. E. H. Smirk, Wigan ; touch judges, Messrs. H. Farmer, Runcorn, end T. Mellowdew, Rochdale Hornets. Warrington had a strong wind at their backs in the opening half, but the Rangers were first on the aggres- sive through Tilley failing to clear. Warrington soon had the ball in midfield, Fish making a fine dodgy rnn almost to the line. Vigorous play was witnessed, and the Rangers came sway with a forward rush which was well stopped by Jenkins. The visitors got possession well and passing on the right was intercepted by Fish who ran clean away to the Broughton full back. A score was expected but Hall just got the Warrington crack by the feet. Warrington were very determined and Brooks getting possession in the Broughton quarter, transferred quickly to Isherwood. The beneficiare dashed between the visitors' centres and romped over the line in great style. thus fittingly opening the score.l Fish kicked a goal. Warrington continued to attack but the passing was hardly so sure as usual and Brooks and Fish were both stopped on the line. Hardyman made one fine run near half-time, but was sent into touch by Tilley. Half-time : Warrington 5 points Broughton nil. On resuming the Rangers at once attacked. Beetham 11 got clear away but missed a glorious chance, and Claude James also hesitated when be should have gone right through. After this Broughton were given little chance, I and except for occasional long punts with the wind had to defend continuously. Brooks made a great run, for Warrington and was pulled down under the posts 1 when a pass to Dickenson would have brought a certain try. Harris kicked a penalty goal from near centre and this was the Rangers' only point. Taylor, Brooks, and Jenkins were all nearly through, but the Broughton defence was sound. Final : Warrington 1 goal, 1 try (5 points) ; Broughton Rangers 1 goal (2 points).

div.head: ISHERWOOD'S BENEFIT.
div.p: ISHERWOOD'S BENEFIT.
Warrington Beat Broughton Rangers.
LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.

WARRINGTON" A" v. BROLIGHTON RANGERS "A."— Played at Broughton on Saturday. The Rangers at once pressed and after smart forward work Scott crossed, Horton failing at the place kick. By superior passing Warrington worked their way to the Broughton quarters, and several efforts to cross were spoiled by the sound defence of the locals. The home forwards bad the better of some tight scrimmages, and forced matters at the Warrington end, where Horton had a futile shot at goal. Warrington rallied splendidly, and another hot raid ended in Forster taking a pass from Kay and placing the sides on equal terms. Turning round for the second half the Warrington backs, especially Jordan, played with sound judgment, and from a good mark the custodian placed the Wire- pullers ahead. The Rangers failed to escape their quarters, and after a neat round of passing initiated by Daintith.Cartwright scored. Maintaining the pressure Kenyon made several capital attempts to break through and he led the way for Watkin to score. The goal kicking was weak. Slater added a try for the Rangers, and then Watkin completed the afternoon's scoring when he raced over for an unconverted try. Final : Warrington, one goal four tries (14 points); Broughton Rangers, two tries (six points).

div.head: ESTIMATES FOR LITHOGRAPHING

The maxim that art and music should go hand in hand is !well-exhibited in the Columbia Phonograph Company's monthly record catalogues, which, in artistic design, are always in happy agreement with the excel- lent musical fare which they announce.
