NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible, not rater than Thursday.

The Mayor and the Nursing Association. am in the very proud position of being able to announce that I have received donations and promises sufficient to pay off the debt of £3OO upon the Warrington Nursing Association and hope to receive sufficient to also pay off the amount of the accumulated interest. Thi3 will entirely relieve the Association from debt and my warmest and heartiest thanks are personally due to those gentlemen and firms who have helped me in raising the requisite sum. I shall be very glad to receive the amounts promised as early as possible to enable me to close the accounts and publish a full list of the subscriptions. Again thanking my friends most cordially for their generosity and assistance.—l am, sir, your obedient servant,
JAMES SMETHURST, Mayor. Town Hall, Warrington. 31st January 1908.

div.head: " Is Interest Robbery ? "
div.p: " Is Interest Robbery ? "

" Thou &bait not be found out."— W. M. Thackeray Sir,—My apology is due to your readers for taking up this discussion alter its being apparently dropped, but not having forgotten the spider to the fly tone of iv r. Parker's letter of the 11th inst., it would be a pity if at least one Socialist bluebottle could not be found to oblige him. Although I cannot compliment Mr. Parker on his logic, I fully recognise the absolute sincerity of all his letters to the Press. An oasis in a desert of humbug and snobbery, it is pleasant and refreshing to find even one gentleman who is openly willing to discuss important questions with working

men. Asa sort of preface, let me say I do not regard the subject of this discussion as a "problem or conundrum," it is too simple to be anything of the kind, and yet, paradoxical though it may seem, only a little lack of knowledge and true grip of human affairs, prevents an affirmative answer being at once given. Further, allow me to say in this discussion I wish to discard all senti- ment, and to take for granted all the elements of human natuie, which, for good or evil, affect both sides of this question. As a basis to my argument, I maintain that usury and interest are one and the same in principle,being tho major and minor elements of a vicious and evil system,invented and perpetuated for the exploitation of mankind. I also contend that he who receives and accepts money which he has not earned, can only obtain it by one of two ways, viz., by gift or theft. Bearing upon this latter statment, as it is manifestly absurd to say that interest is a gift from labour,—the latter not being able to give that which it has not received—it very naturally follows that interest must be the result of theft. I pause here, to note a sentence in Mr. Parker's last letter, to the effect that the question in dispute is not whether labour was robbed, but whether interest was the robber. This admission simplifies the question very much, because if we are inquiring as to who robbed labour, it is pure logic to conclude that labour has been robbed, therefore, I have only to prove the interest- monger to be the thief, and I obtain the verdict. Let me now follow the £lOO which has been invested at 3 per cent. interest. The banker in order to recoup himself as a moneylender, re-loans it to an engineer at 6 per cent. interest. How does the engineer propose to pay back the £6 interest? If Mr. Parker and I were to argue until Doomsday there would remain but one way of doing it, vis., by withholding £6 from the due reward of labour. I anticipate Mr. Parker will say £lOO could be paid for labour and the finished work sold for £lO6 leaving a profit of .t 6 wherewith to pay interest. Now it is not my intention to say much about a trans- action of this kind except to say it relates to another kind of robbery. I also maintain that if £lOO worth of labour is sold for £lO6 it is absolute proof of the existence of another kind of thief. But in anticipating the introduction of the prolltmonger, we must remem- ber we are discussing interest not profit, and it would save both time and trouble if we leave the profit- monger severely alone while we are on the track of the interestruonger. Having given one simple illustration, let me give another as on antidote. Supposing the engineer borrowed £lOO free of interest on his own security to repay in twelvemonths, he could then be able to pay full value for labour, and on completion, could afford to sell at cost price. In this way no one is robbed either by interest or profit, assuming as I do in both cases, that the engineer takes neither more nor less than the reward of his abilities as a brain worker. Finally, as interest cannot be created by either manual or mental labour, so is it scientifically impos- sible to earn it. Interest always did and always will, represent and consist of a stolen quantity which by • right should be paid to labour. I am aware it belongs to the established order of things—so did slavers, and protection a few generations ago—but, ethically and economically, the public mind is slowly but surely becoming alive to its true nature, and—evolution will answer for its abolishment.—Yours truly, RUPERT KETTLE.
30th January, 1908.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
" Aladdin."

One of the best pantomimes which has ever visited Warrington is to be seen at the Royal Court Theatre this week under the management of Messrs. Bottridge and Longden. " Aladdin " and his wonderful lamp form the popular subject, and the story is faithfully adhered to. This much ought always to he conceded for the children's sake. The company is an exceed- ingly strong one and includes three of the best comedians we have seen for some time. Fun is the predominant feature of a very bright and busy show, and the roars of laughter hardly cease for a moment. Mr. Bert Harrow (Abanazar) and Mr. Dick Tubb (Wot-iz-it) are screamingly font y both in song and act. Each introduces specialities of a popular nature and secures encores with the utmost ease. Mr. Joe Robins scores alatost as heavily in the time-honoured Dart of Widow Twankey, who seems to think" it's coming to summatt" and does a lot of excellent foot- ing. Aladdin is impersonated by Miss Fanny Wright, a charming and vivacious principal boy. Her songs, " Jenny," " The Lassie from Lancashire," and "Has anyone seen a Qerman band ? are rendered with a spirit and go which merit the rounds of applause and encores. A capital Emperor is found in Mr. Picton Roxborough, who is an old and accom- plished stage favourite, while Miss Kitty Brewster makes a coquettish Princess Badroulbadour. The Brewster troupe of musical gymnasts and dancers supply several very smart side-turus, and the Brothers Brooks as Chinese policemen are perpetually comical. Miss Flo Collier and Miss Marion Walker also assist in specialities of an attractive nature. Miss Jennie Hallworth makes a hit with" My Aeroplane for Two," while the chorus does its share in presenting a pleasing tout ensemble. The pantominteis splendidly mounted and dressed, no less than eleven different scenes being presented during the evening. There is a matinee to-day at 2-30, and the usual evening performance to-night. We advise intending patrons to go early and make sure of seeing this exhilarating show. The same managers will shortly visit Warrington with a strong Company in "The Village Blacksmith."

div.head: _ NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.
div.p: _ NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

LOCAL PARLIAMENT. OPENING OF THE SESSION. -- Debate on the King's Speech. Our local Parliament in other words the Warring- ton Parliamentary Debating Society - made a success- ful start on Thursday evening. For the nonce the Co-operative Hall. Sankey-street, was transformed into the House of Commons and shortly before 7.30 it was invaded by " honourable members " all bent on settling the affairs of the nation to their entire satis- faction. On a raised platform at the far end of the room was the Speaker's chair and the arrangement of the House followed as closely as possible on the lines of " our prototyped at Westminster " as one budding orator expressed it. To the right cf the Speaker's chair sat the Government supporters. Tne front Bench was reserved for the Ministry, most of whom were in attendance headed by the Premier (Mr. J. Upson). Mr. S. W. Jeffery has now taken up the office of Minister of Education so that the Cabinet is I practically complete. On the left were ranged the Opposition under the leadership of Councillor J. J. Nield while cross benches were reserved for the Socialist and Nationalist , parties, who were there in strong force, atid 'unattached members. At the back, seats were pro- vided for visitors and the large muster of the public testified to the keen interest which was taken in the opening of Parliament. The first business was the election of Speaker, and the choice of Mr. Charles Plinston for that exalted office was one that coin- ! I mended itself to all sections of the House. His elec- tion having been carried with acclamation, the I Speaker, accompanied by the Clerk of the House (Hr. W.Mason),entered and took his seat. Both these gentle- men looked quite dignified and imposing in their wigs ' of office, and on their appearance the House rose to pay its respects. The Clerk of the House and the Secretary of the Society (Mr. Edmund Osborne) were accommodated at a table just below the Speaker's chair. The Speaker having returned thanks and given some good advice as to the conduct of debates, the House got to serious business. The King's Speech, read by the Clerk, promised legislation on licensing, education, old-age pensions, plural voting, railway control and the government of Ireland. Its adoption was moved by two young Liberals (Messrs. H. W. Guest and A. P. Freeman) whose speeches were to the point and earned praise from Government and Opposition alike. The Speech was criti- cised in a mild way by the Leader of the Opposition and a vigorous address be the Premier followed. Representatives of the Socialist and Irish sections gave their views on the Govern- ment programme aud then there was some general discussion from all sides. The proceedings were followed with keen enthusiasm. While a speaker was warmly applauded by his own party, honourable members on the other side smiled superciliously, a,nd gave vent to loud " Oh, Oh's " when the orator said anything which they regarded as particularly out- rageous. It was pleasing to note, however, that the utmost good feeling marked the debate and that oratorical merits were recognized apart from party I bias, many speakers being applauded at the close of their addresses by all sections. There was cue very amusing incident. Alderman Bennett, who occupied a front place in the Opposition ranks, had occasion to leave the House for about an hour. On returning he was unthinkingly crossing the floor of the House to gain his seat, instead of going around-about way to avoid passing before the Speaker. The dignity of the House was outraged, and the Speaker, sternly I regarding the offending alderman, observed in freezing 'tones "Members must not pass before the Speaker! " The alderman looked confused, uttered a hasty apology, and made a dash for his seat, much to the delight of the spectators to whom the incident afforded a welcome break in the ordinary routine. At a quarter to ten the debate was adjourned until next Thursday evening and the House went into committee to discuss questions of procedure. PARTY OFFICERS. Last week we gave the names of the Ministry. The following are the officers of the other parties : OPPOSITION : Leader, Councillor J. J. Nield : Chief Whip,Mr. Herbert Hayes; Junior ‘Vhip,Mr. J.N. Vernon. SOCIALIST GROUP : Chairman, Councillor Stott ; deputy-chairman, Councillor Ball ; Chief Whip, Mr. C. Reeves ; deputy-Whip, Mr. E. Randles. NATIONALIST GROUP : Chairman, Councillor Toole ; deputy-chairman, Mr. M. G. Hearne: Senior Whip, Mr. J. J. Black ; deputy-Whip, Mr. C. Roddy. ELECTION OF SPEAKER. Alderman Bennett was elected to preside over the preliminary part of the meeting. The Premier (Mr. J. UesoN), who was received with cheers, proposed the election of Mr. Charles Plinston as Speaker, and alluded in felicitous terms to his admir- able qualifications for the office. The Leader of the Opposition (Councillor NIELD) seconded, and said he had known Mr. Plinston for 25 I years, and had every confidence in him as an impartial man who, above all else, sought fair play. Conncillor STOTT (Member for Spen Valley) and Mr. M. G. Hearne (Member for Kilkenny South). supported , the proposition which was carried with acclamation. NOTICE OF QUESTIONS. • I The following notices of questions, to be answered next week, were handed in : Mr. W. CIIRIMES (South Birmingham) will ask the Prime Minister whether in view of the rapidly increas- ing numbers of unemployed, the Government will con- sider the advisability of adjusting and reforming our present system of imperial taxation to secure for British traders and manufacturers equal conditions and fair competition in all the markets of the world. Mr. W. H. STANSFIELD (Dublin University) will ask the President of the Board of Education if the grants to denominational training colleges which decline to violate their trust deeds are withdrawn after September next what provision do the Board of Education propose to make in order that those pupil teachers who have been successful in passing the preliminary certificate examination during the current year may receive pro- fessional training. Alderman BENNETT (West Birmingham) will ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether in view of the enormous loss to the Imperial Exchequer which has resulted from the abolition of the coal tax and of the fact that the public generally are paying considerably higher for their fuel, he will consider the desirability of re-imposing that tax. THE SPEAKER RETURNS THANKS. The SPEAKER. then took his seat and thanked the members heartily and sincerely for the honour they had conferred upon him. The Society could congratu- late itself upon the good attendance and upon the fact that they already had 180 members. (Applause.) He hoped that number would during the Session be increased to 250. He asked the members to bear in mind that sound and fury were not argument and that personalities did no good. There was no doubt that the break-up of the old Warrington Parliamentary Debating Society was caused through lack of diplomacy to say the least of it. Argument and argument alone would tell. THE KING'S SPEECH The Clerk of the House then read the King's speech as follows : Gentlemen,—Profound peace extends over the whole world. The blessings of that condition are shared by the people of this country, and the cordial relations existing between ourselves and other nations are a guarantee of the continuance of that happy state. Your attention will have been directed to the unrest in Natal. Whilst upholding the self-goveraing powers of our Colonies we shall be careful to see that native races in these colouies have the full privileges of citizenship. During this session your attention will be directed to several importanp matters requiring urgent attention in home affairs. The Licensing Laws call for reform. All civilised peoples are concerned at the individual, social, and national consequences of excessive indulgence in intoxicants. These nations are experimenting in various ways as to the more effective control of the manufacture of, and the trade in, alcoholic drink, and proposals will be submitted to you by which the local governing bodies shall have greater powers to deal with the manufacture and sale of alcoholic liquors. We consider the time is opportune for introducing a scheme of old-age pensions. Upon the need of these pensions it is not necessary to dwell, but the assist- ance or the House is earnestly requested to devise by which adequate funds may be raised for this
Co-o

Next week Mr. Sidney Benne will present a new and original drama entitled" Love Rules the World This very excellent drama has met with conspicuous success at Liverpool and Manchester, and indeed wherever it has been presented. " Love Rules the World "is a drama somewhat removed from the ordinary type. It is full of incident and a simple and wholesome story is told. There is an interesting blend of love, humour, and pathos. The company is a very strong one, several of its members having already ingratiated themselves with Warrington playgoers by their fine dramatic por- trayals. The cast includes Miss Ruth Shephard, in her original part of the mother, Miss Constance Medwyn, a great popular favourite, Mr. Stephen Langton, who has played with Mr. George Alexander's and Miss Ellen Terry's companies, Mr. Vincent W. Carlyle, late of Mr. H. B. Tree's "The Village Priest" Company, and Mr. Sydney Retina late of Mr. Louis Calvert's principal" Sunday" Company. The scenery and stage effects are on a lavish scale such as is seldom seen in the provinces.
I means

Some doctors spend a lifetime In hunting after germs, And by the time they've killed them, They've grown as big as worms; Microbes would bid adieu to earth, Chest troubles would be fewer, Life would be gay, if everyone Took Woods' Great Peppermint Cure.—Advt.

purpose: The prolonged turmoil over the Education Question, so distressing to all true Educationists, we hope will speedily cease. You will be asked to affirm the principles of the popular contral over schools, and the abolition of tests for teachers. The laws relating to the ownership, valuation, and acquisition of land demand serious attention. We pro- pose to so modify these laws that they shall be brought into conformity with the general interests of the com- munity. We hope to deal with the inequalities of the franchise, by a Bill to overcome the evils of plural voting. We are gravely concerned at the movement towards combination and amalgamation amongst the Railway Companies. We consider this movement to be contrary to the public good, and hope to adopt such measures as will give fuller national control over these great means of communication so vital to our trade and commerce. We hope that before the and of the Session time will be found for the consideration of a measure providing for the better government of Ireland. THE DEBATE. Mt. H. W. GUEST (Accrington) moved the adoption of the King's speech. They must all, he said, be thankful for the peace which at present existed over the whole world, because there could be no greater obstacle

to the general progress of civilization and the social reform of the human race than warfare which was wasteful both in material and in human lives. With regard to Natal, although in view of recent events they could not help feeling that the unrest was very largely due to the action of unscrupulous individuals who might possibly be attempting to alienate the land from the rightful owners, he would ask the House to suspend its judgment until the papers which bed been promised were forthcoming. In the meantime he thought they might trust the Government to use their influence with the Natal Government to prevent the rights of the native races from being infringed. Turning to the clauses which dealt with measures for the social improvement of the people of these islands, there was a further instalment of progressive legislation which was much needed and had been much delayed. If non- members thought their energies were likely to be over- taxed by the numerous questions mentioned in the speech he would remind them that until two years ago, almost twenty years had, he was going to say, been wasted, but he did not know that that could he said. (Opposition "[Tear, hear's.") Unfortunately ! as regarded certain interests, the time had not been I wasted. (Ministerial applause.) During the greater part of that period practically no measures had been I placed on the Statute book which had been directed I towards granting to the country greater equality of opportunity without which it was impossible to calla ourselves a civilized or enlightened nation. The' present Licensing laws were far from satisfactory. (Hear, hear.) Compensation, as it was at present, , without time limitation, was nothing but a ; means of strengthening and confirming the monopoly I which "the trade " held. It was becoming increasingly ' recognized that to give efficient control over the liquor traffic, it was more and more necessary to eliminate private gain and so far as that principle had been adopted by other countries, it could be easily proved that it. had had a beneficial effect in preventing the abuse of what, although it might be necessary, was after all a dangerous beverage. He did not think any- one would doubt the necessity ler the introduction of old-age pensions. (Applause nom the Socialists.) There might be differences of opinion on the details or scope of the scheme but all those would depend upon the funds at the disposal of the Chancellor of the Exchequer. He sincerely trusted there would be sufficient to start a satisfactory scheme, and, if he were not out of place in doing so, he would suggest that there might be a connection between this and the question which had been previously touched upon. The railway companies, continued Mr. Guest, were rapidly approaching if they had not already arrived at a point where competition ceased. The over- lapping of railways was causing great waste and very little practical gain to the public, and there was a great danger of arrangements being brought about which might not be helpful to the traders in their competition with the goods of other countries and would be of very little real use to anybody but the shareholders. While respecting the rights of the shareholders they must not lose sight of the fact that the railways ought to be primarily run for the benefit of the whole cammunity. (Applause.) He scarcely hoped that on two questions which would be brought before them they would not find there existed a political and a deplorable alliance which had been in the past the frequent opponent of progress in the moral, social, and material well-being of the country. (Applause). Mr. A. P. FREEMAN (Chippenham) seconded and said he was pleased that the Government had both the imperial and the parochial view and that the spirit of emancipation pervaded the Speech in regard to colonial and home affairs. Alluding to licensing reform, Mr. Freeman said they might hear that a man must have his freedom to have as much drink as he liked, but he maintained that a man must not have that freedom in the sense in which he had it to-day. They must save the children from the pernicious atmosphere in which many of them existed to-day and give them pure surroundings where they could develop their manhood and womanhood to the highest possible extent. With regard to old-age pensions, he did not know whether any of the members opposite would tell them that those proposals would degrade the people. If so he would ask them to apply to the member who had put the question with regard to tariff reform, to inform them by what subtle and mysterious means an old age pension which when provided by a Free Trade Government was demoralising and degrading, became a priceless boon and ,blessing when provided for by a tariff. (Applause.) Old-Age Pensions were a necessity. (Applause.) He was sure the House would welcome a satisfactory solution of the thorny and delicate subject of education, and he would seriously commend to the Opposition the fact that the time was fast approaching when the people of this country would no longer tolerate the theological hair-splitting and the jangling over dogmas which was keeping theit children from the right and privilege of obtaining a great national and free education,but would say " Away eith this jangling ; away with your fights over creeds and dogmas, and let the children have their right to a free and great education." (Applause.) Councillor NIELD (City of London, and Leader of the Opposition) said it was a pleasure to listen to the eloquent appeals of the Government that something should by done to relieve distress and misery wherever it existed, and he joined with the previous speakers in that wish. Whatever differences they had, he thou 'lit they would all agree that their one great object was the amelioration of the conditions of the people. He was glad to note there was a continuous policy with regard to Imperial affairs, whether the country was governed by a Liberal or a Conservative Government (Ministerial "No's.") He only wished they could see more eye to eye on domestic questions. Whilst he agreed that the motive of the Government might be excellent, it would be his duty as leader of the Opposition to voice the opinion that many of the measures were impregnated with the utmost possible difficulties and in many instances were not likely to secure the result they had in view. With regard to licensing, he considered the Government were going to make a great mistake if they interfered too much with the vested interests. (Laughter.) They had their legal rights and it was not fair to disturb them in those rights. It was a cause for congratulation that the drinking propensities of the people were showing a sensible decrease, and he thought that in removing ignorance and improving education they would do more to bring people away from those habits than they were likely to achieve by any such fad as local option or by putting restrictions on the beer trade. He con- gratulated the Government on having had the courage to put Home Rule on their programme. It was quite obvious to him that the country had no patience with that idea and if the House of Lords ever justified its existence it was when it rejected that memorable Bill which would have granted Ireland home government. The attitude of the Opposition to education and land questions depended on how the details were handled. The reference to plural voting was a pious opinion—a question on which there would probably be differences on both sides of the House. He did not think it was a highly political question and he would pass it by. (Laughter.) It might or might not be a good thing to nationalise the railways. Everything depended on cir- cumstances and on the price they had to pay. Coun- cillor Nield expressed himself in favour of old-age pensions, but said the difficulty was one of ways and means. One thing he regarded as lamentable was that the Government was putting off the evil day in declin- ing to continue the construction of battleships in order to provide old-age pensions at the moment, only making it all the more difficult for his own party when it came back to power to find that all this money that ought to be spent on the navy had been given away in old-age pensions—(Ministerial applause)—and they were confronted with the difficulty not only of having to provide old-age pensions but millions of money for battleships in order to place us in a position of national defence. "There is one question I wanted to touch upon," concluded Councillor Nield, "but as I have lost my notes I will sit down." (Applause.) The Premier (Mr. J. UPSON, Member for Southamp- ton) after expressing his pride in his young recruits who had moved the adoption of the King's Speech, said there was underlying the King's Speech a certain definite principle. They were all agreed upon the necessity of having a happy, prosperous, and contented people. (Hear, hear.) They were all agreed that our people should be sober, well-fed, well educated, and that they should be kept to the last day of their lives without the spectre of poverty intruding into their homes. (Applause.) They agreed that every community had certain primary rights. It had a right to the soil. (Hear, hear.) It had a right to access to the soil, and the right to say that there should be no gathering together of the accumulated stores of labour in the hands of the few—(Socialist cheers )—to be utilized in the oppression of the many. It had a right to say that when its members had served the community faithfully and well they should be kept in comfort in their old age without the taint of poverty. It had the right to say that it would prevent the manufacture and sale of those articles which it had realised by experience were detrimental to its well-being. (Hear, hear.) Over those primary rights there had grown an incrustation of new and class interests. The duty of the Govern- ment was to take away that incrustation and restore those primary rights. While doing justice to all men, the interests and well-being of the community must have the first place. (Applause.) They would no doubt hear the cry of spoliation, but they were not frightened by it. They did not charge the policeman with spoliation when he took from a man who had gained by force the goods of others. (Applause.) The people should have the opportunity of saying whether thev would have in their midst centres of social and moral infection. In whatever direction the progressive tendencies of the Government led them, they would put first of all the well being of the community at large and in a secondary place those interests which in course of time had grown up upon the body politic. (Applause.) The :lovernment believed that subject to the control of the Imperial Parliament, those races under our flag who demanded the right to govern them- selves should have that right, and therefore they had included in their programme a measure giving fuller governmental power to the Irish people. (Applause.) it was true that the late Governmsnt brought before the country the old age pensions question in 1801, but nothing had been done since. The time had come when some attempt should be made to move in that direction. The Government were charged with not being prepared to broaden the basis of taxation. They would broaden the basis of taxation, but the broadening process would not be in the direction in which many of their friends would like them to .o. (Hear, hear.) The broadening was such as would bring under the contributory power,

div.head: GARDEN SUBURBS.
div.p: GARDEN SUBURBS.
PROGRESS OF THE WARRINGTON
SCHEME
Plans Accepted.

The Warrington Garden Suburbs scheme, the object of which is to assist in the solution of the housing problem by establishing suburbs on model lines within easy access of the town, is making headway. A com- pany, known as the Warrington Garden Suburbs Ltd., has the project in hand, and two suitable sites have been acquired at Great Sankey and Grappenhall. En order that the sites might be developed to the best advantage, plans were invited and 21 sets were sent in. The competition resulted in the selection of the designs, for the planning of both estates, of Messrs. A. and J. Soutar. 59, Westover-road, Wandsworth, London. The plan for the Grappenhall estate sent by Mr. E. Prentice Mawson. Haylewood Offices, Windermere, obtained second place, and that of Mr. Basil C. Deacon, of Liverpool, for the Sankey site, also secured honour. able mention. An exhibition of the whole of the plans entered for competition was opened at the Old Academy on Monday afternoon, and will continue until 9.30 this (Saturday) evening.. At the opening there were present :—Mr. C. E. Parker (chairman of the company), Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson, Mr. W. Peter Rylands and Mr. Arthur Bennett (directors, the last-narced being the secretary), Mr. F. R. Roberts (one of the company's solicitors), and Mr. E. J. Hall (Messrs. Henry Greenalt and Co. ; also solicitors to the com- pany), and Mr. Seger Owen. Mr. C. E. PARKER, in opening the exhibition, said the object they had in view when they formed the company was that they should be able to set an example in providing facilities for better, and healthier homes for the people,and not to do S) purely on philanthropic lines but in the direction of helping people to help themselves. The trend of thought and action in regard to public affairs at present was very largely in the direction of calling upon the State to do everything we want, depending on State aid and giving over to State control. The tendency seemed to be that we should get into the position in our national affairs of everybody leaning one upon the other. He did not think the tendency was altogether good, although it might be so far good. It was very liable to ran to extremes. What they should aim at in their public effort was so far as possible to develop individuality of character. He did not think there was any better way in which they could aim at that than in doing what they were trying to achieve in regard to garden suburbs—that was to create healthy conditions an which the home life could have its free and natural development. In the home the strongest qualities which made for healthy individualism could be created and nurtured. When they considered the homes in which many of those in Warrington had to live—he did not mean particularly those houses which were called slum dwellings, but the general character of the long, dreary monotonous roads in which the bulk of the people lived —surely something better could be achieved. They were confident that by the garden suburbs scheme they would be able to show that the dwellings of the artisan classes could be such that the people would be disposed to take more pride in their homes which would then ,ecome more of a reality to them. The directors or the company did not expect to introduce Utopia in the town but they could show the way, and he hoped that as the garden suburbs developed they would make the people ashamed of many of the houses that one now saw. The very fact that there were these better surroundings and homes would set ,an example to all who thought of building and thus raise the whole level of the character of building in Warrington. They had a great variety of designs sent in and, with the help of Mr. bear Owen, they had been able to choose what they considered to be very much the best designs for both estates. (Applause.) Canon MoRLEY STEVENSON, in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Parker, said he bad been at the backbone of the movement and had supported it in every way, both by his purse and his hard work. He (Canon Stevenson) had all along felt that the only way by which they could improve the towns was to capture the suburbs, for the suburbs of to-day were the towns of to-morrow. One thing which had attracted him very much to the winning plans was that they did not ' provide for ono class of building only, but for large ' houses as well as small, and it was this great idea that they should try to receive the typical village life where rich and poor lived together. They should not be all one class of peaple living in one spot, for he belivered very much in the mixture of the classes in some given locality. (Applause.) Mr. W. P. RYLANDS seconded. All who had been associated with the movement, he said, knew to what extent they Were indebted to the great assistance and energy which Mr. Parker had extended in that work. It was a work worthy of anyone's best efforts because if one could imagine the time when the whole of War- rington would be surrounded with suburbs of the kind illustrated on the plans they would feel that Warrington would be very different from what it was to-day. It this movement had begun fifty years ago it was quite possible the result he had mentioned might have been achieved to-day and we would be living in a town surrounded with pretty suburbs and the working people would be dwelling in cottages with surroundings which would be far more satisfactory and elevating than the present conditions. The success or otherwise of the movement must depend upon the manner in which it was received by the people of Warrington. If Warring- ton were not at its back, the movement must meet with comparative failure. The company was not a purely money-making speculative company, but it was one in ; which,while provision was made for a reasonable, small rate of interest, the rettirn was strictly limited and any profits over and above that would go entirely to the improvement and development of the estate and to the advantage of the tenants. (Applause.) Alderman BENNETr, in supporting, said they had one of the most influential and representative bodies of Directors he had seen in connection with any local company. They had been working quietly for some months and now they came out into the open and invited the co-operation of the public. As time progressed he believed the investment would be a sound one and pro- duce a reasonable return. The experiment, however, would not be a success unless they had the co-operation of the working-classes in whose interests the movement was primarily intended. They had been working for months to establish a Co-operative Tenants' Society on the lines which had been so successful at Ealing and elsewhere, and they hoped within a few days to have the new Company registered and to be able to invite 11 the support of the working-classes. His only regret in I regard to the plans was that the local firm had not been successful, but that could not be helped and he cordi- ally thanked them for competing. (Applause.) The vote was heartily accorded. In responding, the CILA.IRAIAN said some confusion had arisen in the minds of many as to the Co-operative Tenants' Company, the prevalent idea being that the Garden Suburbs Ltd. was going to build the whole of the houses upon the estates on the lines which had been adopted by the Tenants' Company. Tnat,was not so for as far as that company was concerned, they were wining and wishful that builders and private individuals should take part of the land. All that the Company laid down was that anyone building should conform to the reason- able conditions which would be formulated. THE SELECTED DESIGNS. The plans sent in represented a wide range of design, from the usual building type of lon. uninteresting streets, with similar style of houses and general design, so well known in large town suburbs, to designs which show an extravagance of outlay in recr,,r;--

div.head: DEATH OF MR. S. M. CROSFIELD. An Old Lancash ire Cricketer.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. S. M. CROSFIELD. An Old Lancash ire Cricketer.

Many of our readers will deeply regret to hear of the death of Me. S. H. Crosfield, cousin of the Member for Warrington, which took place at the Hotel Metropole, Las Palmas, on Thursday. The deceased gentleman was very well known in Warring- ton where at one time he was a prominent figure in the realm of cricket. He was the son of the late Mr. Morland Crosfield, of Lymni, who was one of the three sous of the late Mr. Joseph Crosfield, the founder of the firm of Messrs. Crosfield and Sons, Limited, the well-known soap manufacturers at Warrington. Taking, as he did, no part in public affairs, his name will long be remembered by all who entertain an interest in cricket. Born in 1801, Mr. Crosfield from an early age entered with zest into the absorbing national pastime, and though he never attained really gteat distinction in either of the chief departments of the I game, he was for many years recognised as a thoroughly good " all-round " man. In local cricket he displayed the keenest interest, and the Warrington Club, of which he was for many years captain, owes much of its position and success to his initiative and enthusiasm. Mr. Cros.ield's first county experience was with Cheshire —a shire which now boasts no irepresentative team —but he soon joined forces with Lancashire, and rendered the Palatine long and yeoman ser ice. On many occasions he acted as captain o the Lancashire team, and his great knotvledg of the game, coupled with a ripe judgment of men, often enabled him to secure victory for his side. As a batsman, he was what may be termed one of the fearless type, getting runs when they were sorely needed. It was in the fielding department where perhaps he excelled, his work at "mid off " add " extra cover "' being one of the best features. Whilst connected with the Warring- ton Club from about 1878 to 1888 he certainly assisted in bringing the club to a high 'state of excellence sufficient to place it amongst the leading senior teams in the county. Mr. Crosfield gave up active participa- tion in the game more than ten years ago, and to the younger generation his sterling performances are pro- bably unknown. Older followers of the game will recollect, however, how much he did to encourage " colts "and to select them for Lancashire. Latterly, Mr. Crosfield took to golf, and played that game also with characteristic sportmanship. The deceased gentleman was also noted as a pigeon shot, and for two years in succession lie was second for the great pigeon shooting prize at Monte Carlo.

"UNDE,R THE RED ROBE." Dramatic Society's Forthcoming Per formances. During the week commencing February 10th, the Royal Court Theatre will be occupied by the Warringtm Dramatic Society who will present the romantic play in four acts a' Under the Red Robe." This is certainly the most ambitious enterprise which the Society has undertaken, and we have reason to believe that the production will maintain the Society's best traditions. With the artocratic Cardinal Richelieu as the dominating figure, the play is full of dramatic incident and excitement and we should advise all Warrington playgoers to make a point of seeing it. No fewer than 45 players will be engaged in the performances which will lack nothing in com- pleteness. The bulk of tha scenery will be new for the occasion and the costumes will be by Messrs. L. and H. Nathan, of London, who had charge of the idressing of the London production of the play. The cast is as follows Gil de Berault Mr. Charles H. Wood Cardinal Richelieu Mr. H. G. Mosley Marquis de Porubal Mr. Victor Roberts Do Faris Mr. R. P. Johnson Captain Larolle Mr. Sidney Wallhead The Lieutenant Mr. \V. Owen Smith Sir Thomas Brunt Mr. H. Chambers Clon Mr. H. G. Mosley Louis Mr. J. Craik Sergeant Mr. Harvey Adams Henri de Cocheforet Mr. Victor Roberts Renee de Cocheforet Mrs. Robert Garnett Madam de Cocheforet 'Miss Bessie Pierpoint Madam Zaton Miss Mary Brundrett Suzette Miss Rose Wallhead Waitresses f Miss Wallhead 1 Miss Bessie Richardson In the course of the play, Gregorian music (specially arranged by Mr. J. Eckersley, organist of St. Mary's Church) will be sung by Mr. F. Fieldhouse and party. The proceeds of the performances will be devoted to the Warrington Infirmary Extension Fund and the Children's Summer Camp Fund, and we hope the public will readily avail themselves of the opportunity of aiding these most worthy objects and at the same time witnessing an entertainment which is sure to delight them. The plan of reserved seats opens to-day at Mr. H. M. Ashton's, chemist, Sankey-street. •

div.head: CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
Corcert at Latchford

-- In order that the Latchford members of this Society may reaNthe benefits of the Education Committee of the Society, a concert was held in the Parish Room, Latchford, on Thursday. when there was a large attendance. Mr.J. W. Bouchier presided in the absence of Mr. William Landor, who was away on business in connection with the C.W.S. Mr. BOUCIIIER, at the outset, said some younger people in the audience were no doubt looking forward to the time when they could become members of their Society. There were two reasons why they should become members First, because they icould not run in debt, as their Society demanded cash down on every article. The members could not get goods and have a bill sent in which had been running for a long time. Secondly, because at the end of three months there would no doubt be a few little things they required, and which they could get from the dividend. (Applause.) The concert then commenced with a pianoforte solo entitled ' lieroudelles " which reflected great credit on Miss Kilduff, who also sang " Abide with me " in a very pleasing manner. Mr. W. Kilduff was deservedly and loudly applauded for his recitals "An old Bachelor,' Christmas Day in the Workhouse," which is a very pathetic piece, and " My uncle " the music of which was especially written for the late Sir Henry Irving by Sir Charles Benedict. Mr. and Miss Kilduff were heard to distinct advantage in the duet " Excelsior "and gave as an encore "Alice where art thou " in capital style. The Co-operative Male Voice sang" Comrades in Arms" for which they were heartily encored. A duet entitled " The moon bath raised her lamp " was followed by a quartette entitled "The old Kentucky home " by the Apollo Male Voice Quartette,who gave as an encore" The teacher and the tack " whieh was smartly rendered and very amusing. The Male Voice Choir gave " Tom, the piper's son "in very creditable style. Much praise is due to the able conductor of the choir, Mr. Albert TrOW.

--- - The CHAIRMAN. after the entertainment was over, said they must express the very great pleasure they had had in listening to the entertainment and toMr.and Miss Kilduff and especially to their own Male Voice Choir. (Applause.) He thought they were a good looking lot. (Laughter.) If they must have a good choir they must have a good leader and that they certainly had in Mr. Albert Trow. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Trow had always done his duties as leader of the choir in a very ei-Mcient manner. They must also express their thanks to Mr. Rushton, the secretary of the Education Committee, who had worked very hard indeed during the winter in gettin g those entertainments together. (Applause.) The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. RUSEITO,..:, in reply, said they could not thank him Setter than by turning up in large numbers. The object of the Education Committee was to provide their members with good entertainments and lectures which would be of great educational value to them.

A River Mystery. At 12.15 on Sunday morning Mr. Thomas Crompton, 52, St. Mary-street, Latchford, was returning home when be heard cries of " Help " from a man who had evidently fallen into the river Mersey near the Corpora- tion Wharf., Howley. Mr. Crompton immediately informed P.C. Chrimes, who proceeded to the scene with him and Sergeant Dean. Chrimes also heard a cry for help, and then be noticed a man struggling in the water, which was carrying him away. The officer boarded one of the flats and procured a boat hook, but this was of no use as the man had got out of reach. However, farther down the river George Cliffe, captain of the fiat Alert, lying in Bishop's Wharf, threw out a rope. This the man failed to grasp, and disappeared. Sergeant Dean and Constable Chrimes have made inquiries in the neighbourhood without being able to ascertain whether any person is missing.

WARRINGTON. Life of Crime. John Shaw, alias Adam Turner, was sentenced to two months hard labour at Warrington, on Saturday, for being found on the enclosed premises of Fred Doraville, in Knutsford-road, early on hursday morning. Police Constable Edwards found him crouching in the yard. He failed to give a satisfactory account of himself and made several rambling state- ments. -The Chief Constable said Shaw had been 1 sentenced to between thirty and forty years' penal servitude. All his previous convictions were for burglary. Shaw's defence was that he had no intention of committing any robbery. He said he was drunk at the time; but the constable said he was shamming. Eckersley) and Madame Christian, and Messrs. J. Sephton and R. A. Robinson treated the audience to several songs, and they also gave a quartette in excel- lent style. Ar. and Mrs. Sephton were very successful in several duets. The Warrington Concertina Qnartette Party won golden opinions with their splendid playing. The humorist was Mr. Pearson. Mrs. B. Wycliffe P.S.A. Mr. B. Farrar presided at a meeting of the Wycliffe Society on Sunday afternoon, and read a letter from Canon Willis thanking the society for the vote of sympathy sent to him in his great trial, and stating that it was to him a great comfort to receive expressions of sympathy from all denominations in the town. Mr. J. Ewan, of Sale, gave an address upon "Forgetting the things that are past and reaching forward to the things before." He urged the members not to be too satisfied with their past wcrk, but to press to the goal. Mr. Payton rendereu an organ solo to the delight of the brethren. Mr. D. Owen and Mr. R. Beswicicalso took part in the meeting. Progressive Labour League. The annual meeting in connectton with this League was held at the Liberal Club on Monday evening under the presidency of Mr. T. At the opening meeting of the second half of the Winter Session which was presided over by Mr. F. Womersley, Mr. Dunlop contributed an inter- esting account of the emergence from the egg of the young of the common lizard. He also exhibited a jar, intended for museum use, showing (preserved in spirit) the lizard, its eggs; and the young. Mr. Fuller delivered a lecture, entitled " The evolution of a bulb." There was a short but lively discussion, during which allusion was made to the various modes of growth and reproduction amongst so-called bulbous-rooted plants, and a brief reply to his critics by the lecturer concluded a very enjoyable evening. A Woman's Violence. At the Borough Police Court on Saturday, Alice Quinn was sent to gaol for four months, on charges of wilful damage, obscene language, and assaulting the police It was stated by Mr. Awbery (Workhouse Master), that the woman was admitted to the work- house from Winwick Asylum. On Friday morning she demanded her immediate release, and refused to do any more work. Because her request could not he granted she created a scene and made use of violent language. Her violence was so great that she had to be placed in a cell, where she smashed the windows and door. Police-constable Leonard was called in, and, whilst being conveyed to the police station in a cab she struck him in the face with her fist several times, and kicked him about the legs. 'LINSEED COMPOUND' of 40 years' proven ecfficay for Coughs, Colds, and Bronchial troubles.—Advt. Silver-street Senior Men's Bible Class. In connection with this class an open meeting was held in Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church on Sunday afternoon, when the members, accompanied by a fair number of friends, attended to receive the prizes for the last half-year. Mr. John Upson, the leader of the class, presided in the absence of Mr. Frank Harris, and the speaker was the Rev. J. F. Matthews, who congratulated Mr. Upson upon his election as premier of the local debating society, and said that his class should feel that they had had a signal honour bestowed upon them. Mr. Matthews spoke of the racial problem, and said he believed the time was coming when the brotherhood of man would be recognized. Mrs. Upson distributed the prizes. Local Teacher's Success. The distinction of obtaining first place in the first class (mistress's division) in the National Society's examination in religious knowledge of candidates for admission into Church Training Colleges, held on October 26th, 1007, has been achieved by Kathleen M. Cole, one of the pupil teachers of Fairfield school. She was prepared by the Vicar of St. Barnabas' (Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth). The examination was open to all England and eleven hundred and four girls were examined, of whom Si) passed in the first class, 720 in the second, 247 in the third and 42 failed. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge offers a prize varying from £5 to /I to each pupil teacher who takes a first class at the above examination, and subsequently enters a Church Training College as a residential or day student. For future examinations a prize of £lO will be given to each of the first sixty successful candidates in order of merit, whether boys or girls. LINSEED COMPO UND,' Trade Mark of Kay Co mpound Essence of Linseed for Coughs Sc Colds.--Adv Rev. H. Dunnico and Mr. Blatchford. The Rev. Herbert Dunnico, speaking at Whitefield- road P.S.A. on Sunday afternoon, said his Socialism was the practical outcome of his study of Jesus Christ. Jesus Christ was the greatest Socialist the world had ever seen. For 1,800 years there has been a competi- tive system. What was the result ? The strain of , life was greater, the rich were becoming richer, the ' poor were becoming poorer. Life was never so strenuous as today. There were many senses in which the people were better off, but life was so strenuous. It was impossible to be loyal to Jesus Christ in the present. competitive system, and if a system prevented a man from being loyal to Jesus Christ, the sooner that system was eliminated the better. Socialism meant that all the means of produc- tion, all the agencies of production and distribution, should be owned and controlled by the people for the benefit of the people. The Socialist is a man who did not believe in private monopoly. With regard to Robert Blatchford, Mr. Dunnico believed that Robert Blatchford was an utter ignoramus upon religion. He did not know what he was talking about, he was not qnalified by study, he was ignorant of theology. He bad no right to speak with authority on the subject of the Christian religion. But there was no Christian man in England to-day who had done more to educate and interest the masses of this country in subjects which were intended to better their lot. 'LINSEED COMPOUND' for Coughs and Cold Relieves Asthma and difficult breathing.—Advt. Sankey Wire Mills Cricket Club. The annual meeting and supper in connection with the above club were held on Saturday night at Atkinson's Cafe, Bridge-street. A good muster of members put in appearance and after full justice bad been done to an excellent repast the business was proceeded with. Councillor J. Hawthorn presided. The report of the Secretary (Mr C. E. Hawthorn) showed that the club had had a fairly successful season ; out of thirteen matches played, six were won, , six lost, and one drawn. A spacious portion of the new ground in Longshaw-lane,had been specially laid, the cost of which was defrayed by the proceeds of a drawing. The prospects for the coming season were very rosy and it was expected that the club would maintain its prestige in junior cricket The fixtures for the ensuing season had been arranged and were calculated to provide excellent cricket. The financial statement submitted by the treasurer (Mr. H. L. Clarke) showed a balance in hand of :5.:2 Bs. 7d. which was considered very satisfactory owing to the large outlay caused by the transference of the club to another ground, and the provision of a playing pitch. The president (Mr. E. Houghton) was re-elected and also the other officials including Mr. W. Woodcock, captain first team; Mr. H. Clarke, 3ub-captain. -On the conclusion of the business, musical items were rendered by Messrs. N. Cook, W. Barnes and P. D. Bailey

" HEART LIKE STONE." Lazy Man Sent to Gaol for Neglect of Children. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday ( before the Mayor and other magistrates, James Deverenx, 2, Hopwood-street, was charged with neglecting his three children in a manner likely to ' cause them unnecessary suffering and injury to health. Prisoner pleaded not guilty. Mr. Arthur Browne, who prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C.,said that the prisoner and his wife occupied two back rooms of a four-roomed house in Hopwood- street. Perhaps the magistrates might say " Why not prosecute the wife ?" Well, the wife had been left on several occasions and the Society had had reports through their officers and the case against the woman had been withdrawn. The prisoner would not work and he would not get up to go to work when he had it. He had been earning ISs. a week at, Dallam but through his laziness he had lost the job. He had not been near the house or helped his children in any way whatever for three weeks. When Inspector Cox visited the house he found that they occupied the two back rooms of the house. The children were ravenously hungry. There was an apology for a bed in the shape of an old mattress which was in a sort of a recess in the day time and was brought out at night. Inspector Cox discovered that the husband had never been near the house for some time and at once sent for Mr. Aukland who ordered the family's removal to the Workhouse. I Inspector Cox, of the N.S.P.C.C., corroborated all that Mr. Browne had said and said that the man had not been near the house for three weeks and had been getting his food at a coffee house whilst his wife and family got nothing. He looked after himself. Mrs. Devereux, wife of the prisoner, said she was quite willing to give evidence. Her husband had never been near the house for a fortnight. He left the children starving, and she had to pawn all the furniture to get food for herself and the children. He worked when be liked, and if he thought be would have a day or even a week off he would have it. She had no food in the house last, Tuesday. The Mayor said the prisoner did not feel his position at all. John Constable said the children were in the Work- house hospital suffering from neglect. The woman had two articles of clothing cn, and amongst the three children there were only eight articles on them when they were admitted to the Workhouse. Ti was a bad Case. The prisoner when asked if he had anything to say said that he had been out of work. When he was at home his wife would not get up to light the Pre or get him any breakfast. The Chief Constable said the prisoner had been eighteen times previously convicted, but the majority of the cases were for not sending his children to school, The Mayor said the prisoner had a heart like a stone. He ought to have been ashamed of himself. He would have to go to gaol for three months with hard labour. _ PEN KETH.
